The two language workloads are decoder-only causal LMs trained on a deterministic 100M-token FineWeb-Edu subset with context length 256: a 17.7M-parameter micro model and a 33.6M-parameter small model, each trained for 5,000 optimizer steps with an effective batch of 16 sequences. The two vision workloads use a 2.70M-parameter ViT on balanced CIFAR-100 and a 100:1 long-tailed CIFAR-100 variant. Muon is applied only to hidden attention and feed-forward matrices, including fused QKV projections. Embeddings, normalization parameters, biases, and output heads use auxiliary AdamW. In the two language models, Muon covers about 26.7% and 42.2% of parameters. The Muon update maintains matrix momentum and applies five quintic Newton-Schulz iterations after Frobenius normalization, producing a direction that approximates the UV^T factor of the momentum matrix. Each workload uses a one-seed, 23-candidate development budget. The selected configuration is then evaluated with five matched seeds, full validation trajectories, CUDA event timing, and a frozen one-shot test protocol.c:T48e,Instead of only comparing four binary transitions, AdamW-to-AdamW, AdamW-to-Muon, Muon-to-AdamW, and Muon-to-Muon, the paper constructs mixed optimizers. At each update step, it samples a Muon update with probability p and an AdamW update otherwise, with p in 0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, and 1.0. This turns optimizer identity into a continuous axis and enables a p_PT by p_SFT grid. The score in each cell is decomposed into a global mean, a pretraining row effect, an SFT column effect, and a residual interaction term. If matching optimizers had an intrinsic benefit, the residuals should be systematically better along the p_PT = p_SFT diagonal; the experiments do not show a strong pattern of that kind. The continued-pretraining experiments use the same logic and show that apparent switching costs largely disappear after learning-rate tuning. AdamW uses decoupled weight decay and gradient clipping. Muon follows the paper’s Algorithm 2 and uses the 0.2 RMS update scaling from prior Muon work. The authors also use the expected update RMS for AdamW with beta1 = 0.9 to align update scales and allow a common base learning rate across mixture settings.d:T45f,The main controlled experiments train 1.2B-parameter Llama-3-style models from scratch, with 32 layers, 24 attention heads, full multi-head attention, and hidden size 1536. Pretraining is run at 1x and 8x Chinchilla scales, corresponding to roughly 24B and 193B tokens, using the data mixture from Wen et al. 2026. SFT uses the Tulu-3 mixture for two epochs. Sequences are packed to 4096 tokens for the 1.2B models and Llama-2-7B, and to 8192 tokens for Qwen models. Evaluation covers MMLU, BBH, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MBPP. The 1x Chinchilla PT-SFT optimizer grid is evaluated with three random seeds per pairing. The main empirical findings are that increasing the fraction of Muon updates during SFT generally improves downstream performance regardless of the pretraining optimizer, optimizer-matching residual gains are small, and optimizer consistency reduces pretraining-distribution forgetting without producing a corresponding downstream advantage. The paper also fine-tunes AdamW-pretrained open-weight Llama and Qwen models up to 14B parameters and finds Muon competitive with AdamW for task-general SFT.e:Ta2b,技术路线可以概括成一句话：用 streaming k-PCA 持续追踪梯度主子空间，并把上一时刻的子空间和优化器状态平滑迁移到下一时刻，而不是周期性从零开始重估。

先看问题设定。对某个权重矩阵层，梯度 g_t 是高维的。GaLore 类方法会维护一个低秩基 U_t，把梯度投影到这个 rank-k 子空间里，在低维空间中做 Adam 类更新，再映射回原空间。难点在于 U_t 需要跟着训练变化。GaLore 的做法是隔若干步做一次 SVD 重算，这样每次更新 projector 都像一次 cold restart：旧子空间信息被丢掉，Adam 一阶二阶矩也很难自然继承。OSD 则通过额外优化过程去适配移动子空间，但实现更重，也更难稳定。

Ori 的核心判断是：如果 U_t 与 U_{t-Δ} 在小 Δ 下通常很接近，那么最合理的做法是 warm-start tracking。具体实现上，作者采用受 Oja++ 启发的 streaming k-PCA 更新。每一步都用当前梯度对已有基做轻量旋转，使基逐步贴近新的主方向。其单步代价是 O(dk^2)，相比频繁做全量 SVD 要轻得多，因而可以支持高频甚至 gap-free 的 projector 更新。

但仅仅更新基还不够。低秩优化器真正容易出问题的地方，是基变了以后 optimizer state 怎么办。Ori 在这里加入 drift-aware bootstrapping：把上一时刻子空间基作为当前初始化，并对 Adam 风格的一阶矩、二阶矩做跨基转移。这样做的直觉是，如果子空间只是小角度旋转，那么旧统计量并没有失效，直接丢弃会造成不必要的优化震荡。文中的 drift coefficient ρ 用来控制 carry-over 强度，实验显示 ρ≈0.99 较好，说明“保留连续性但不过度僵化”是有效区间。

从算法结构看，Ori 不是把低秩空间当成静态压缩容器，而是把它当成一个随训练动态演化的状态变量。这个视角与 GaLore 的周期重算有本质区别：GaLore 更像 snapshot estimation，Ori 更像 online tracking。与 OSD 相比，Ori 不依赖额外的非凸追赶过程，而是直接利用 streaming PCA 的结构更新，因此计算和实现都更干净。

理论部分给出了带 drift 的 dynamic regret 分析。作者证明在 noiseless setting 下可得到 sublinear dynamic regret，且对相邻时刻子空间漂移量的依赖较温和。这个理论不是全文最重要的部分，但它至少说明 Ori 的设计不是纯经验拼装：当子空间连续漂移时，在线跟踪而非反复冷启动，确实能得到更合理的误差累积性质。f:T4d6,This is directly relevant to pretraining. First, it reframes low-rank optimization as a training-dynamics problem rather than a pure compression trick: the bottleneck is not only low rank, but stale projectors. Second, it gives a practical answer for memory-constrained pretraining: if the gradient subspace drifts slowly, then frequent, lightweight, continuous updates are better matched to the dynamics than infrequent, heavy recomputation. Third, the gains appear in the very low-rank regime, which is where these methods are actually hard. At generous ranks many approaches work reasonably well; the real test is when each projector dimension is expensive. On 1B LLaMA pretraining, Ori reduces the gap to full-rank Adam by up to 69.3% under a rank-128 optimizer state versus embedding dimension 2048, while remaining compute-efficient. That makes the contribution operational, not merely conceptual.

The contribution spans three layers: an empirical characterization of gradient-subspace drift, a new optimizer design, and drift-aware theoretical guarantees. It does not replace mainstream full-rank training, but it is highly relevant for memory-limited pretraining, continual training, and the broader study of low-rank optimizers.10:Tb1b,The method can be summarized as follows: continuously track the principal gradient subspace with streaming k-PCA, and smoothly transfer both the basis and optimizer statistics across time instead of repeatedly re-estimating the subspace from scratch.

Consider a weight matrix whose gradient at step t is high-dimensional. Gradient-subspace methods maintain a rank-k basis U_t, project the gradient into that subspace, perform an Adam-like update in low dimension, and map the update back to the full space. The hard part is keeping U_t aligned with the current gradient geometry. GaLore handles this by periodic SVD refreshes, which behave like cold restarts: previous subspace information is discarded, and optimizer moments do not naturally carry over. OSD moves toward continuous adaptation but does so through an additional non-convex optimization loop.

Ori starts from a different empirical premise: if U_t is close to U_{t-Δ} for small Δ, then warm-started tracking should be more efficient than repeated re-estimation. The paper instantiates this with a streaming k-PCA update inspired by Oja++. At each step, the current gradient induces a lightweight rotation of the existing basis, nudging it toward the new principal directions. The per-step cost is O(dk^2), much cheaper than frequent full SVD, which makes high-frequency or effectively gap-free projector updates feasible.

A second key piece is optimizer-state continuity. Updating the basis alone is not enough, because low-rank optimizers also maintain first and second moments in the projected space. Ori introduces drift-aware bootstrapping: the previous basis initializes the current one, and Adam-style moments are transferred across successive bases. The intuition is simple: if the subspace only rotates slightly, then old moments are still informative, and resetting them would inject unnecessary optimization noise. The drift coefficient ρ controls how much carry-over is preserved; empirically, a small but strong carry-over around ρ≈0.99 works well.

Conceptually, Ori treats the low-rank subspace as a dynamic state variable that evolves with training, not as a static compression container. That is the main difference from GaLore’s snapshot-style recomputation. Relative to OSD, Ori avoids an extra non-convex catch-up loop and instead uses a structured streaming PCA update, which is cleaner computationally and algorithmically.

The theory section provides dynamic-regret guarantees under drift. In the noiseless setting, the paper derives sublinear dynamic regret with mild dependence on the consecutive drift parameter. This is not the main reason to read the paper, but it does show that the design is not purely heuristic: when the target subspace moves continuously, online tracking has a better cumulative-error story than repeated cold restarts.11:T795,The experiments are organized around two settings: LLaMA-1B pretraining and RoBERTa-Base finetuning.

The pretraining result is the main one. On a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, Ori is tested in a very low-rank regime where the optimizer-state rank is 128 while the model embedding dimension is 2048. This is a stringent setting and a good stress test for projector staleness. The headline result is that Ori reduces the performance gap to full-rank Adam by up to 69.3% relative to prior low-rank baselines. The paper also presents a performance-memory frontier where Ori sits on the favorable lower-left boundary, indicating better accuracy under low memory and low compute.

For finetuning, the paper evaluates RoBERTa-Base across 16 scenarios with even smaller ranks, 8 or 4. Ori outperforms competing methods in 10 of the 16 cases. The gains are less uniformly dominant than in pretraining, which is unsurprising given higher task variability and noisier optimization in finetuning.

The ablations are especially informative. Increasing the projector update period consistently hurts performance, directly quantifying the cost of staleness. This is one of the strongest pieces of evidence in the paper because it isolates the mechanism behind the gains. A second ablation shows that adding a small carry-over, with drift coefficient around ρ≈0.99, improves accuracy, confirming that moment transfer is not a cosmetic detail but a core part of the optimizer. The paper also measures gradient-subspace drift empirically and shows that after warm-up, neighboring subspaces remain close over short windows, which supports the streaming-tracking premise.

From a pretraining-engineering perspective, the most useful takeaways are not just the benchmark wins but three empirical rules: gradient subspaces drift slowly, stale projectors are especially costly at low rank, and preserving optimizer-state continuity is better than repeated resets.12:T698,This one is worth a careful read. A good order is: phenomenon, algorithm, ablations, then theory.

Start with the introduction and the beginning of the optimizer section. The first thing to verify is whether the paper really establishes that gradient-subspace drift is slow and stable rather than noisy and discontinuous. The whole method depends on that claim. Then read the algorithmic core: the modified Oja++ or streaming k-PCA update, how the projector is refreshed at high frequency, and how first and second moments are transferred across successive bases. While reading, keep asking two questions: why is periodic SVD the wrong abstraction here, and why is moment transfer justified instead of dangerous?

In the experiments, prioritize the LLaMA-1B pretraining table and the performance-memory figure, then the ablations on update period and drift coefficient ρ. Those sections make the mechanism most visible. If time is limited, the theory can be deferred. If you work on optimizers, the dynamic-regret section is still worth reading because it formalizes the slow-drift tracking view.

The figures and tables most worth studying are the subspace-drift measurements, the performance-memory frontier, the comparisons against GaLore, OSD, LoRA, and full-rank Adam at different ranks, and the ablations on update frequency and carry-over strength. Expected reading time is 60–90 minutes. Good follow-up questions are whether Oja-style tracking remains stable under noisier gradients, whether moment transfer accumulates mismatch over very long runs, and whether the slow-drift assumption still holds for larger models, longer token budgets, MoE training, or changing curricula.13:T631,Muon can be interpreted as normalized steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry, implemented through a linear minimization oracle over a spectral-norm ball. BMuon modifies that oracle. For hidden channel j in block ell, it couples the corresponding row of the MLP up-projection with the corresponding column of the down-projection, and assigns an allocation μ_j^ell in [0,1]. All such channels across all MLP blocks share a single budget K, with sum_{ell,j} μ_j^ell = K. For a fixed allocation, BMuon inserts a diagonal reweighting into Muon’s spectral-norm constraint. The allocation is then chosen globally to maximize first-order loss decrease, so channels across layers compete for the same budget rather than being controlled by fixed layerwise sparsity targets. The paper shows that the resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a norm Ω_{α,K}. The parameter α controls the strength of channel reweighting, and K controls the global channel budget. The construction recovers Muon when α=0 or K=N. At α=1, the unit ball becomes the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most K coupled hidden channels. At α=K=1, it reduces to an l1-style aggregation over channel groups. This differs from NuMuon: NuMuon targets low-rank compressibility through a nuclear-norm constraint, while BMuon targets structured hidden-channel compressibility. Since exact allocation would be expensive at every step, the practical algorithm uses a minorization-maximization surrogate for the allocation update, followed by a weighted Muon update.14:T442,Its relevance to pretraining is mainly through training mechanics rather than language modeling objectives. The contribution is not a new LM loss, but a different answer to the memory wall: change the gradient pathway itself instead of only compressing or recomputing activations. That matters for three reasons. First, it pushes local learning from a mostly empirical idea toward a gradient-estimation framework with theory, at least for deep linear networks and residual nonlinear networks near the right regime. Second, the locality definition is operationally meaningful for large-model training: only one block’s activations need to be kept at a time. Third, the LLM finetuning results suggest that first-order local gradient surrogates can beat zeroth-order methods under similar memory budgets, which is a useful signal for low-memory adaptation. The limitation is equally important: the evidence is not yet large-scale from-scratch LLM pretraining. So this is better viewed as a promising training paradigm candidate than as a drop-in replacement for standard pretraining recipes.15:T77d,The method, ProxyProp, partitions a deep transformer into gradient-isolated blocks. For block l, instead of waiting for gradients to flow through all downstream blocks, the method attaches a local proxy network that takes the block output h_l and predicts the final network output. The proxy is trained by distillation against the global model output. The block update is then computed by backpropagating through the proxy, not through the actual downstream stack.

The central idea is not merely to add an auxiliary head. The proxy is meant to estimate the downstream input-output Jacobian seen from that block. In deep linear networks, the paper argues that an optimal linear proxy implicitly recovers the expected linear map from the current representation to the final output, making the local gradient exact. For nonlinear residual networks, the analysis depends on residual parameterization: when skip connections dominate, the downstream mapping is close to identity plus a small perturbation, so the proxy-induced gradient error can be bounded; at initialization, the local gradient can even match the true gradient exactly. This is the main reason the method is positioned for modern residual transformers rather than arbitrary deep architectures.

Operationally, each block can be updated immediately after its forward pass, satisfying the decoupled or unlocked learning setup. Memory savings come from avoiding full-network activation storage and retaining only the local computation graph for one block plus its proxy. Compared with classic local-loss training, ProxyProp is trying to predict the effect of the remaining network on the final output, rather than forcing each block to solve the task directly. Compared with zeroth-order methods such as MeZO, it still uses gradient information, but obtains it through a local surrogate, which is why it can be more compute-efficient at similar memory cost.16:T672,The experiments appear to have two main parts. The first is supervised learning with vision transformers, used as a controlled setting to study the memory-accuracy trade-off under different block partitions. The reported takeaway is that ProxyProp dominates prior local learning baselines across partition choices: for a given memory budget it achieves better accuracy, or for a given accuracy it uses less memory. The important pattern to inspect is how performance degrades as the model is split into more blocks and locality becomes stronger. The claim is that ProxyProp degrades more gracefully, which would support the gradient-approximation story.

The second part is memory-efficient LLM finetuning. Here the comparison to MeZO is the key result. The paper states that ProxyProp achieves better downstream performance at comparable memory cost, even when MeZO is allowed roughly 8x more compute time. That is a meaningful comparison because zeroth-order optimization is often considered when memory is extremely constrained, but it suffers from high variance and slow convergence.

The currently available text does not expose enough full tables to restate every concrete number with confidence, such as exact ViT sizes, datasets, partition counts, or the LLM parameter scales and task suite. When reading the full experimental section, three details are worth checking carefully: whether memory accounting includes optimizer state and proxy overhead, whether runtime is reported as wall-clock or FLOPs, and whether the LLM finetuning updates all parameters or only PEFT-style modules. That last point changes the practical significance a lot.17:T404,For a skim, start with the definitions in the introduction: locality, decoupling, and unlocked training. Those tell you what class of methods the paper is actually competing with. Then go straight to the theory sections on two claims: why the proxy gives exact gradients in deep linear networks, and why the error remains controlled in nonlinear residual networks under residual parameterization and skip-dominant regimes. Those sections carry most of the paper’s intellectual weight.

In the experiments, focus on three items: the accuracy-memory curves as the number of blocks changes, the ablation on proxy design, and the fairness of the LLM finetuning comparison against MeZO. A useful reading question is whether the gains come mainly from a better local target or from enabling a more favorable memory/parallelism regime. That distinction determines whether ProxyProp should be thought of primarily as an optimization method or as a systems-facing training alternative. A solid skim should take around 30 to 45 minutes.18:T927,方法上不是提出全新量化格式，而是把近一年 NVFP4 训练 recipes 的关键设计轴拆开做 controlled comparison，并在此基础上拼出一个组合配方 Mosaic NVFP4。核心技术点集中在三块：

1）选择性高精度层（selective high-precision layers）
- 论文明确把它当作“必要条件”来检验：即便其它量化细节都优化，仍需要把一小部分敏感层（通常是 embedding / output / normalization / 或少数关键投影层，具体以实现为准）保留在更高精度（如 BF16/FP8）以避免规模上去后的不稳定与尾段质量差。
- 这里的关键不是“混精度”本身，而是它在 FP4 噪声很大的 regime 里承担了类似数值锚点（anchor）的作用：减少误差在深层堆叠与长训练中的累积。

2）反向量化：无偏梯度估计 + 降低 backward quantization error
- 论文把“梯度估计偏差会在长 horizon 累积”作为主线，比较了不同 backward-pass 处理：包括 MS-EDEN（Quartet II 提到的 unbiased estimator）与其它随机舍入/随机旋转类方案。
- 结论是：在“全层量化”的设定下，选择性地对梯度使用 MS-EDEN，再对其余 backward tensors 用 Four Over Six 的 scale 选择，能得到测试中最小的 loss gap。这说明：无偏并不需要对所有张量一刀切，成本/收益可以分层配置。

3）前向/反向 scale 选择与 1D/2D 权重量化的耦合
- 现有 recipes 的分歧点之一是：NVIDIA ’25 recipe 倾向 2D 权重量化以保持 forward/backward 权重表示一致；而 Quartet II / 随机旋转类方法更自然地配 1D 量化（沿 contraction 维度），并通过“forward 权重 dequantize 后再按 backward 维度 re-quantize”来近似一致性。
- 论文的 Mosaic NVFP4 选择把这些拼起来：在 backward 两个 GEMM 上都做 Random Hadamard Transform（降低量化误差/偏差的结构性相关），梯度用 MS-EDEN 保无偏，其余张量用 Four Over Six 做更好的 scale 选择，同时保留选择性高精度层。

整体上，这篇的创新不在某个单点技巧，而在于把“前向表示质量”和“反向无偏/低偏梯度”两条路线的冲突点（1D/2D、权重一致性、旋转的放置位置）用统一实验回答：哪些组合在 1T tokens 的尾段仍站得住。19:T6d6,Rather than proposing a new numeric format, the paper decomposes NVFP4 training into major design axes and evaluates combinations systematically, then proposes a composite recipe (“Mosaic NVFP4”). The approach has three pillars:

1) Selective higher-precision layers
Ablates whether leaving a subset of sensitive layers in BF16/FP8 (e.g., embeddings/output/norm or other critical projections depending on implementation) is necessary. The paper argues this acts as a numerical anchor in the FP4 noise regime, preventing instability and late-stage degradation that persists even with otherwise strong quantization tricks.

2) Backward pass: unbiased gradient estimation + reduced quantization error
The backward pass is treated as the main long-horizon risk: biased gradient estimators can accumulate over training. The study compares unbiased estimators (MS-EDEN from Quartet II) and related techniques, and finds that selectively applying MS-EDEN to gradients while using Four Over Six scale selection for remaining backward tensors yields the smallest observed loss gap when all layers are quantized.

3) Coupling between scale selection and 1D/2D weight quantization
Existing recipes disagree on 2D quantization (to keep forward/backward weight representations consistent) versus 1D schemes (more natural for rotation-based bias reduction). The paper highlights the practical workaround used by 1D schemes—dequantize forward-quantized weights and re-quantize along the backward contraction dimension—and builds Mosaic NVFP4 by combining: selective high-precision layers, Random Hadamard Transforms on both backward GEMMs, MS-EDEN for unbiased gradients, and Four Over Six scale selection for other tensors, while staying kernel-compatible.1a:T562,Key experimental choices are “medium scale + long horizon + unified stack”:
- Models: dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE (Nemotron family). The dense setting includes a hybrid Mamba-Transformer variant (24 Mamba-2 layers, 4 attention layers, 24 FFN layers).
- Training horizon: up to 1T tokens, explicitly to surface late divergence.
- Data: phased blending (diverse data for the first 600B tokens, higher-quality thereafter).
- Ablation axes: selective high-precision layers; forward/backward scale selection; 1D vs 2D weight quantization; backward bias mitigation (random rotations/Hadamard, unbiased estimators); and their interactions.
- Reported outcome-level findings (directional from the provided full text excerpt):
  (1) omitting selective higher-precision layers can trigger instabilities and prevents full BF16 recovery at larger scale/medium horizons;
  (2) MS-EDEN (for gradients) + Four Over Six (for other backward tensors) gives the lowest loss gap among tested fully-quantized backward configurations;
  (3) Mosaic NVFP4 (HP layers + dual backward-GEMM Hadamard + MS-EDEN + Four Over Six) achieves the strongest BF16 loss-gap result at this scale while remaining compatible with efficient kernels.

Exact numeric gaps/throughput/energy figures should be taken from the main result tables and late-stage loss curves; the excerpted sections do not include the numbers.1b:T4b8,How to read it efficiently at depth:
1) Start from the recipe matrix/table that enumerates variants across forward/backward, 1D/2D, HP-layer choices, unbiased gradients, and scale selection. Without this, later curves are hard to interpret.
2) Focus on the second half of training (toward 1T tokens). The paper’s central claim is late-stage divergence; early checkpoints are misleading.
3) Read the backward-bias section carefully: what MS-EDEN corrects, why rotations/Hadamard are applied to both backward GEMMs, and how this interacts with 1D/2D quantization and weight “consistency”.
4) Inspect the selective higher-precision layer ablations: which layers are kept high precision, what fraction of compute/memory they represent, and how much stability/quality they buy.
5) If you care about transferability, check whether trends hold across dense vs MoE and across hybrid Mamba-Transformer vs more standard blocks.

Good follow-up questions to investigate while reading: whether HP layers mainly stabilize forward representations or reduce backward noise amplification; and which gradient paths dominate the need for unbiased estimation (implied by the fact that MS-EDEN can be applied selectively).1c:T9cd,方法核心是“最终层共享的因果自递归”。作者沿用 DeepSeek-V3 那类 causal MTP 的基本思想：第 k 个未来位置的预测，要依赖前一步预测出的 token，因此保持未来 token 之间的因果依赖，而不是像早期 parallel MTP 那样从同一个隐藏状态独立预测多个未来位置。不同之处在于，ECHO 不再为每个 horizon 单独挂一个预测模块，而是把 backbone 的最后一个 decoder layer 反复拿来用。具体做法是：从当前位置的最终层隐藏状态出发，结合上一步预测 token 的 embedding，通过一个轻量 fusion layer 连接，再递归应用同一个 final decoder layer 和同一个 output head，逐步生成更远 horizon 的预测。除了这个轻量 fusion 层，未来预测所用参数与 next-token generation 完全共享。

这个设计带来两个机制上的变化。其一，监督路径改变了。辅助 MTP 中，depth-2、depth-3 的损失主要训练各自的附加模块；ECHO 中，所有 horizon 的损失都直接更新负责 next-token 的最终层参数，因此多步监督更集中地塑造 backbone。其二，训练-推理形式一致。因为同一层本来就被设计成可递归调用，所以推理时可以自然继续往更深 horizon draft，而不是受限于训练时显式存在的几个辅助头。

为了解决深 horizon 训练成本和噪声问题，作者又引入 Dynamic Depth Sampling（DDS）。不是每个样本都算到固定最大深度，而是按随深度衰减的分布采样每一步递归深度。这样做有两个考虑：一是把平均训练开销降下来，文中给出的 amortized overhead 约为 1.5 个 depth-1 step；二是更深 horizon 的 teacher signal 本身更噪，因为前面预测误差会累积，越深越可能把错误上下文喂回模型。用衰减采样，相当于承认“深监督有价值，但边际收益和信噪比会下降”，因此让训练更多落在浅层、少量覆盖深层。

从与已有方法的区别看，ECHO 不是简单的 parameter tying。关键不只是省参数，而是把 multi-horizon objective 的受益者从 auxiliary head 改成 backbone 本身。与 DeepSeek-V3 式 causal MTP 相比，它保留了因果未来建模，但去掉了 horizon-specific 模块；与 parallel MTP 相比，它显式建模未来 token 之间依赖；与 post-hoc drafter 路线相比，它把 draft 能力直接预埋进预训练权重，而不是事后再为推理速度单独调一个 drafter。1d:T861,The core idea is efficient causal self-recursion with final-layer sharing. Like DeepSeek-style causal MTP, ECHO preserves autoregressive dependence across future horizons: the prediction at horizon k depends on the previous predicted token rather than predicting all future positions independently from the same hidden state. The key change is that ECHO does not attach a separate prediction module for each horizon. Instead, it recursively reuses the backbone’s final decoder layer and output head.

Starting from the final-layer hidden state at the current position, the model combines the previous predicted token embedding with the previous hidden state through a lightweight fusion layer, then applies the same final decoder layer again to produce the next horizon. This process repeats for deeper horizons. Except for the fusion layer, all parameters used for future prediction are shared with standard next-token generation.

This changes where the learning signal lands. In auxiliary MTP, depth-2 and depth-3 losses mostly train the newly added horizon-specific modules. In ECHO, every horizon loss updates the same parameters that generate the next token. The claim is not merely parameter efficiency; it is that direct multi-horizon supervision should shape the backbone more effectively.

To make deeper supervision affordable, the paper introduces Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS). Instead of always training to a fixed maximum depth, the recursion depth is sampled from a decaying distribution. This reduces amortized compute and also addresses a modeling issue: deeper horizons carry more accumulated prediction error and noisier supervision. The decaying schedule reflects that deeper targets are useful but lower in signal quality. The paper reports an amortized overhead of about 1.5 depth-1 steps.

Relative to prior work, ECHO differs from parallel MTP by preserving causal dependence across future tokens; it differs from DeepSeek-V3-style causal MTP by removing horizon-specific heads; and it differs from post-hoc drafter approaches by baking drafting ability into pretraining rather than finetuning a separate drafter later.1e:T7bc,The most important experimental evidence comes in three parts. First, under matched prediction depth, ECHO outperforms auxiliary causal MTP. The paper reports gains already at depth 1, especially on math, reasoning, and code: about +0.79, +0.57, and +1.35 respectively. At depth 3, the gap widens further, reaching about +2.63 on reasoning and +2.23 on code. This supports the claim that the benefit is not simply from predicting more tokens, but from where the supervision is applied.

Second, the paper asks whether deeper supervision continues to help. Averaged over 14 benchmarks, increasing depth from 1 to 3 improves ECHO by 0.63 points, while DeepSeek-style auxiliary MTP improves by only 0.16. This is a central result. It suggests that the limited gains of deeper auxiliary MTP are not because long-horizon supervision is inherently unhelpful, but because the added losses are mostly absorbed by the extra modules. The paper also connects this observation to MiMo, which reported weak returns from stacking more MTP layers.

Third, ECHO is evaluated for speculative decoding. Because the same final layer is recursively reused, the model can draft directly with pretrained weights and does not require drafter finetuning. More importantly, acceptance remains strong when drafting beyond the training depth, and acceptance length keeps improving under depth extrapolation, whereas auxiliary MTP saturates earlier. The paper emphasizes that this matters most in realistic high-entropy generation, where post-hoc drafters often overfit to benchmark-style distributions. It also notes that after supervised finetuning, ECHO’s advantage over auxiliary MTP becomes larger, especially on reasoning and code.

A strong part of the experimental design is that it separates two questions: matched-depth comparisons test whether final-layer sharing is better than auxiliary heads, while within-family depth scaling tests whether added horizons are actually being used effectively.1f:T5c7,Start with the method figure and focus on the computation graph difference between auxiliary causal MTP and ECHO. The important point is not parameter tying by itself, but the relocation of the training signal: who actually learns from multi-horizon losses. Then read Figure 3(a) carefully. It is one of the main pieces of evidence because it shows both matched-depth comparisons and the gain from increasing depth within each method family.

Next, read the DDS section with two questions in mind: why use a decaying depth distribution instead of a fixed maximum depth, and how much of the benefit comes from compute reduction versus noise control at deeper horizons. If you care about training recipes, pay attention to how amortized overhead is computed and how different depth distributions trade off cost and quality.

For inference, focus on the acceptance-rate and acceptance-length curves under depth extrapolation, and compare them with post-hoc drafters. The interesting question here is why recursive final-layer reuse extrapolates better. A plausible interpretation is that ECHO learns an iterative generation operator, whereas auxiliary heads learn horizon-specific mappings.

If time is limited, a good reading order is: introduction, method figure, Figure 3(a), DDS, and speculative decoding experiments. That is enough to capture the main claim in under an hour. Read the ablations and post-SFT results if you want to judge whether the method is worth reproducing.20:T451,The system uses a hybrid eager/compiled design. It avoids a JAX dependency in the runtime and accesses TPUs through PjRT, with StableHLO and Mosaic as compiler entry points. On the PyTorch side, it supports roughly 450 ATen operators, including forward and backward paths for the Core ATen ops needed by major model families. The compiled path is based on Torch Dynamo and torch.compile rather than Lazy Tensors. The eager path introduces DeferAndFuse, a runtime strategy that delays and fuses operations to reduce the gap between op-by-op execution and fully compiled execution. Distributed support is provided low in the PyTorch stack through TPU collectives and ProcessGroup integration, enabling DDP, FSDP, and DTensor-style workflows. Custom kernels can be written through JAX/Pallas and Helion DSL. The design also emphasizes bounded dynamism to reduce XLA recompilation caused by shape changes. The TPU execution model has important consequences: the MXU favors sufficiently wide tensor shapes, and a TPU device can be accessed by only one user-space process, which complicates RL-style colocation.21:T8ce,The algorithmic proposal is DP-Muon, but the real contribution is the analysis. Muon can be viewed as applying approximate orthogonalization to momentum for matrix-valued parameters. More abstractly, it fits into a linear minimization oracle (LMO) framework. This unifies Muon with Scion, SignSGD, and normalized SGD as different geometries of direction selection over norm balls.

The key theoretical observation concerns the expected clipped gradient, μ(g)=E[clip_c(g+ξ)]. The paper shows that it can be decomposed into a positive scalar multiple of the true gradient g plus a residual term r(g) that changes direction. Since an LMO is invariant to positive rescaling, LMO(λg)=LMO(g) for λ>0, the dominant effect of clipping is invisible to the update rule. Only the directional residual enters the optimization error, and that residual is controlled by the centered gradient variance. This is the central idea of the paper. It avoids the usual strong assumption of bounded raw per-example gradients and does not require the clipping threshold to grow with the horizon.

Building on that decomposition, the authors derive a convergence guarantee for private momentum-LMO methods on smooth nonconvex objectives in any finite-dimensional norm. The bound separates optimization error, momentum tracking error, sampling noise, privacy noise, and a clipping floor. The floor scales as ρ1 min{σ, σ^2/c}, where ρ1 is the norm-conversion constant into the relevant dual norm. The interpretation is that passing clipped gradients through an LMO costs at most a geometric conversion factor relative to clipped SGD, rather than introducing a qualitatively new instability. At fixed noise scale, the rate is about O~(K^-1/4); with noise calibrated to an (ε, δ) privacy budget, the dependence matches the familiar DP scaling.

Algorithmically, DP-Muon still follows the standard central example-level DP pipeline: per-example clipping, Gaussian noise addition, averaging, then momentum and Muon orthogonalization. Privacy comes entirely from the first stage; the optimizer-specific part is post-processing. The novelty is therefore not a new privacy mechanism, but an explanation of why Muon-style post-processing remains analyzable under active clipping.22:T5e6,The empirical study has two parts: validation of the theory’s implications and optimizer comparisons under DP. The experiments cover CNNs and a 30M-parameter GPT language model, with sweeps over batch size, learning rate, and momentum, comparing DP-SGD, DP-Adam, DP-Muon, and Scion. Two findings stand out. First, under DP the optimal batch size shifts upward by one to two orders of magnitude relative to non-private training. That alone is an important recipe change. Second, optimizer ranking becomes batch-size dependent; unlike the non-private setting, where Muon tends to dominate more consistently, there is no single winner across the DP regime.

On CIFAR-10, DP-Muon achieves the lowest mean test loss at all but one batch size, although at intermediate batch sizes the gaps are often within one standard deviation. So the advantage is real but not overwhelming. On language modeling, DP-Muon is best at small batch sizes, DP-Adam is strongest near the optimal batch size, and Scion performs best at large batch sizes. This is consistent with the theory: once clipping and privacy noise interact, geometry, momentum dynamics, and batch-dependent noise scale jointly determine which update rule is preferable.

If the full paper provides more detail, the most useful pieces for LLM researchers are the GPT setup, the privacy budget, the token budget, and the computational overhead of Muon’s orthogonalization. The language-model batch-size sweeps are much more informative than the vision results.23:T541,For a skim, start with Section 3. The goal is not to absorb every proof, but to understand two claims clearly: clipping mainly induces a positive rescaling along the true gradient, and an LMO is blind to that rescaling, so only the directional residual matters. Once those two points are clear, the rest of the theory becomes much easier to place. Then read Theorem 1 and the surrounding discussion to see how the error terms are separated, especially the clipping floor and the role of ρ1.

For experiments, prioritize the language-model results over the vision section. Look first at the batch-size sweeps, then at the optimizer comparisons near tuned hyperparameters. A useful skim should take around 25 minutes. For a deeper read, include the appendix discussion against concurrent work, especially the distinction between centered-variance assumptions and raw-gradient moment assumptions, and why this paper does not need a clipping threshold that grows with training horizon.

Three follow-up questions are worth keeping in mind. Can the LMO perspective extend to hybrid AdamW/Muon recipes used in large-model training? Is the norm-conversion constant too loose in high-dimensional matrix settings? And since the language-model experiment is only a 30M GPT, how far these conclusions extrapolate to billion-scale pretraining remains open.24:T5a3,t-Muon constructs 3rd-order tensors from groups of related Transformer gradient matrices and applies a transform-based tensor SVD framework:
- Tensorization choices: the paper evaluates multiple ways to stack gradients into tensors, including Layer-wise stacking, QKV grouping, Head-wise grouping, and Head-stack variants. The intent is to couple updates where Transformer structure suggests shared statistics.
- M-transform: an orthogonal transform along the 3rd mode (identity/DFT/DCT/DST), which mixes frontal slices and defines the tensor algebra (t-product) used by t-SVD.
- Update rule via t-SVD: in the transform domain, the tensor decomposes into independent frontal slices; t-Muon effectively applies Muon’s polar/Orth operation slice-wise in that domain and then transforms back. This yields an update that is provably steepest descent under the corresponding transform-induced tensor spectral norm.
- Theory: establishes the steepest-descent property for the exact update and provides a non-asymptotic stationarity guarantee for an idealized stochastic tensor method with Nesterov-type momentum. In implementation, polar factors are approximated (e.g., Newton–Schulz iterations), similar to practical Muon.
Compared to prior tensor-aware Muon extensions that orthogonalize unfoldings, t-Muon’s coupling is controlled by the transform choice rather than a fixed matricization, making the design space more explicit and tunable.25:T6a8,The method is simple by design. The authors argue that Adam’s second-moment state contains substantial local redundancy, while the first moment carries richer directional information and is much less compressible. AdamPM therefore applies pooling to the moment states with the main focus on second-moment pooling. Adjacent entries are grouped along either the row or column dimension, and each group shares a single mean statistic instead of maintaining element-wise second moments. The resulting preconditioner remains diagonal in form, but its granularity becomes group-wise rather than per-parameter. The paper motivates this with empirical statistics collected during LLaMA 130M pretraining. The second moment has much lower effective rank than the gradient or the first moment, suggesting that its information is concentrated in a small number of dominant directions. Local coefficient-of-variation measurements also show stronger similarity among nearby second-moment entries, making them suitable for sharing. By contrast, the first moment has higher effective rank and is more sensitive to pooling because it largely determines update direction. Based on these observations, AdamPM keeps Adam’s first-moment update and overall update rule, while replacing the storage and estimation of the second moment with pooled statistics. The paper also provides a convergence analysis and introduces cosine similarity and relative error to measure how closely AdamPM matches vanilla Adam in terms of preconditioners and parameter updates. A notable claim is that this approximation becomes better as model scale increases, which would make the method more attractive for larger models rather than less.26:T625,From the provided full text, the experiments span LLM pretraining, language-model finetuning, and vision-language model finetuning, with three main questions in mind: memory reduction, performance retention, and hyperparameter portability. The analysis section is built around LLaMA 130M pretraining and reports effective-rank and coefficient-of-variation statistics for embeddings and transformer matrices such as key, value, and MLP gate projections. The main empirical takeaway is clear: the second moment is much more structurally redundant than the first moment, which justifies compressing only the former. The paper also compares pooling the first moment versus pooling the second moment and finds that first-moment pooling hurts performance more and deviates more strongly from Adam’s update trajectory. Another important result is that AdamPM can inherit Adam’s learning rate and beta settings directly, avoiding the recipe retuning that often blocks adoption of new optimizers. The authors also emphasize that the method introduces little to no training-time overhead, which matters because many memory-saving optimizers trade memory for extra kernels or communication. While the excerpt does not include the full result tables, the text highlights a useful intermediate finding: as model size grows, cosine similarity between AdamPM and Adam updates increases and relative error decreases. If the main training curves support that trend, AdamPM looks less like a new optimization regime and more like a scale-friendly state-compression approximation to Adam.27:T61a,The paper formulates score mismatch as a perturbation of the reverse rate matrix in the continuous-time Markov chain underlying discrete diffusion. This differs from the continuous diffusion case, where mismatch is often expressed as a perturbation of the reverse Gaussian mean. The analysis gives a non-asymptotic KL upper bound between the target distribution and the sampler distribution. The bound separates the intrinsic sampling error from an additional bias term induced by using the training-distribution score for a mismatched target distribution. The mismatch term is tied to a Bregman divergence associated with score entropy, rather than a plain L2 score error.

The paper then applies the framework to Conditional SEDD. The common hard-clamping procedure resets observed coordinates to their fixed values at each reverse step. The analysis shows that this operation is not universally equivalent to the true conditional reverse process. Under an absorbing rate and fixed non-MASK observations, the hard-clamp score matches the true conditional score on unobserved coordinates, so no extra score-mismatch bias appears in the bound. Under a uniform rate, this equivalence generally fails.

For coordinate-wise set constraints, the paper uses a mixture over feasible assignments. Once an assignment is chosen, the fixed-observation sampler can be reused. This gives a way to extend fixed-observation guarantees to general set constraints while separating the error from conditional sampling and the error from approximating the assignment distribution.28:T51a,The controlled dense experiments use looped models with 730M stored parameters and 2.9B unrolled parameter applications. Each looped model stores 28 Transformer blocks but executes a logical path of 112 block applications. The Ouro-style baseline is R28^4: a 28-block stack repeated four times. The Huginn-style model is P8 R12^8 C8: an 8-layer prelude, a 12-layer tied recurrent core repeated eight times, and an 8-layer coda, again totaling 112 logical block executions. Two feedforward anchors are used: D28, matching resident parameters, and D112, matching logical depth with independent parameters. The ablations show that the sandwich envelope gives the clearest gains, especially on math, context extraction, and reasoning-heavy tasks. Input injection improves knowledge retrieval and prompt-context utilization, but can hurt some quantitative reasoning. Random initialization is not consistently useful, and separate high/low recurrent states add complexity without dependable improvements. The full Huginn design outperforms Ouro on all ten dense benchmarks. In MoE experiments matched by resident and active parameters, Huginn again beats Ouro, balances expert load better, uses different experts across loop iterations, and approaches a larger feedforward MoE while storing far fewer parameters.29:Tca2,论文先给理论分析，再给 LED 机制。

第一部分是对 MDM 与 UDM 的优化差异做 ELBO 分解。沿用 path-space ELBO 的写法，目标可拆成 transition prediction loss 和 schedule matching loss。标准 MDM 的 forward transition 是朝 mask token 的吸收过程，schedule 与 denoiser 无关，因此 schedule matching 项为零；模型只需学好反向预测。UDM 的 forward/reverse 过程则涉及全词表上的替换，等价地会引入一个依赖 denoiser 的 schedule matching 项。这个项不是常数，而是模型相关的额外误差源，所以 UDM 的 excess loss 更大，也更难优化。这个分析给出了“为什么 MDM 往往更稳”的明确理由，而不是经验判断。

第二部分是表达能力分析。作者用 circuit complexity 来刻画并行模型的计算深度。结论是：即便允许 arbitrary-order prediction 和双向注意力，标准 MDM 仍停留在 TC0 这一常数深度并行计算类里，和 AR 模型在复杂度层级上相近；UDM 因为允许 rewritable state，可以通过多轮重写实现更深的层级计算，达到 TC0 并支持 NC1 级别的层次化计算，例如求值嵌套布尔表达式。这里的重点不是复杂度标签本身，而是“可重写中间状态”带来了真正不同的计算机制。

LED 的设计正是围绕这个结论展开。它不改 MDM 的 commit 机制，而是额外引入一个 proposal branch。训练时，先用一个预训练 MDM 生成 proposal sequence，再把 proposal 作为条件输入，训练 LED 模型用标准交叉熵去预测目标 token。由于 proposal 里既有对的 token，也有错的 token，模型被迫学会两件事：什么时候保留 proposal，什么时候编辑 proposal。这里没有引入 UDM 那种模型依赖的 diffusion schedule，仍然保持 MDM 风格的简单监督。

推理时，LED 在每个 commit stage 内部交替执行 proposal stage 和 commit stage。proposal stage 维护一个可重写的中间状态，允许 token 在多个 lookahead steps 中被反复生成和修正；commit stage 则遵循标准 masked diffusion，一旦某个 token 被提交，就在后续 stage 中固定不再改写。这样，rewritability 被限制在 proposal 分支内部，而最终输出路径仍然是 MDM 式的逐步提交。跨 stage 时，已经验证较可靠的 proposal token 会被保留，错误 token 则在后续 proposal 中继续修正。

这个结构的关键取舍很清楚。为什么不直接训练 UDM？因为那会把 rewritability 放进主生成过程，训练目标更难。为什么不只做普通 MDM？因为 commit-once 机制限制了迭代修正。LED 选择把“可改写”放在辅助分支，把“可训练”留在主分支。它更像是在 MDM 外面包了一层 lookahead editor，而不是把整个模型改成 uniform diffusion。

从实现角度看，LED 也不是简单 reranking。proposal branch 不是只给一个草稿，而是在每个 commit stage 内部多步迭代，形成真正的中间可编辑状态；commit branch 则利用这个 refined proposal 作为额外条件，决定哪些 token 现在值得锁定。这个 proposal/commit 解耦，是全文最值得反复琢磨的设计点。2a:Tcee,The paper first develops the theory, then introduces LED.

The optimization analysis starts from the path-space ELBO for discrete diffusion. The objective can be decomposed into a transition-prediction term and a schedule-matching term. In standard MDMs, the forward process is an absorbing transition toward a mask token, and the schedule is independent of the denoiser, so the schedule-matching term vanishes. The model only needs to learn reverse prediction. In UDMs, transitions operate over the full vocabulary, and the schedule effectively depends on the denoiser, introducing an extra model-dependent schedule-matching loss. This creates additional excess loss and makes optimization harder. The paper therefore gives a principled reason, not just an empirical one, for why MDMs tend to train more easily.

The expressivity analysis uses circuit complexity. The key result is that standard MDMs remain in TC0, even with arbitrary-order prediction and bidirectional attention. In other words, their parallel computational depth stays constant because committed tokens cannot be rewritten. UDMs, by contrast, maintain a rewritable state and can repeatedly revise tokens, which enables richer hierarchical computation and supports NC1-style behavior. The exact complexity labels matter less than the underlying mechanism: rewritable intermediate states fundamentally change what the model can compute in parallel.

LED is built around this observation. It keeps the MDM-style commit process intact, but adds a proposal branch that is allowed to rewrite tokens. During training, a pretrained MDM first generates a proposal sequence. LED is then trained, with standard cross-entropy, to predict the target sequence conditioned on that proposal. Because the proposal contains both correct and incorrect tokens, the model must learn when to preserve a proposal token and when to edit it. This preserves the simple supervision of MDMs and avoids introducing a UDM-style model-dependent diffusion schedule.

At inference time, LED alternates between a proposal stage and a commit stage within each commit block. The proposal stage maintains a rewritable intermediate state, allowing tokens to be generated and revised over multiple lookahead steps. The commit stage then follows the standard masked-diffusion process: once a token is committed, it is fixed and cannot be changed later. Across stages, reliable proposal tokens are preserved, while erroneous ones are revised in future proposal iterations.

This is the central design trade-off. Why not train a UDM directly? Because rewritability inside the main generative process makes optimization harder. Why not stay with a plain MDM? Because commit-once decoding limits iterative correction. LED places rewritability in an auxiliary branch and keeps trainability in the main branch. It is better understood as a lookahead editor wrapped around an MDM than as a uniform diffusion model.

Implementation-wise, LED is also more than draft-and-revise reranking. The proposal branch is iterated inside each commit stage, creating a genuine editable latent text state. The commit branch uses the refined proposal as additional conditioning to decide which tokens are safe to lock in. This proposal/commit decoupling is the most important design idea in the paper.2b:T783,The experiments use Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-8B as backbones, trained on the same data with either standard MDM SFT or LED SFT. Evaluation covers eight benchmarks across math, code, and science. The headline result is strong and simple: LED SFT improves over standard MDM SFT by +11.4 average points for Qwen2.5-7B and +7.7 points for Qwen3-8B. The paper also reports that LED-8B, trained with SFT alone, outperforms LLaDA2.1-16B Q-Mode, which uses continued pretraining, SFT, and RL. That suggests the gain is not a minor tuning effect but a meaningful shift in effective capability.

The mechanism-facing experiments are especially useful. The paper studies the number of lookahead editing steps, the quality of the proposal sequence, and the interaction between proposal and commit stages. The general pattern is that moderate iterative revision helps, but returns do not grow without bound, which supports the interpretation that the proposal branch provides a revisable intermediate state rather than unlimited extra compute. The paper also shows selective editing behavior: high-quality proposal tokens are often preserved, while incorrect ones are revised. This is evidence that the model is learning to edit, not merely to ignore the proposal.

The complexity discussion is accompanied by synthetic or structured tasks illustrating the benefit of rewritable state for hierarchical computation. Even if those tasks are not the main benchmark story, they help explain why gains are especially visible on math and code, where iterative correction of intermediate structure matters more than one-shot commitment.

From a pretraining and modeling perspective, the most important empirical fact is this: with the same backbone, same data, and same SFT budget, changing the modeling and decoding structure alone yields 7–11 point average gains. That is strong evidence that the expressivity bottleneck of plain MDMs is real.2c:T693,This one deserves a careful read in the order of motivation, mechanism, and evidence.

Start with the introduction and the ELBO analysis. The key question is why the schedule-matching term is zero for MDMs but model-dependent for UDMs. That explains why the paper does not simply move toward a UDM.

Then read the circuit-complexity section. Even if you do not follow every proof, make sure to understand the conclusion: commit-only generation limits computational depth, while rewritable state enables more hierarchical parallel computation. This is the most unusual part of the paper, and also the part that gives the strongest conceptual explanation.

Next, study the LED method figure and the training/inference procedure carefully. You want a precise picture of the proposal stage, commit stage, lookahead steps, and how tokens are preserved or revised across stages. It is easy to misread LED as a simple draft-then-edit system, but the actual design is more structured: an editable proposal branch is maintained inside each commit stage.

In the experiments, prioritize the main table, the comparison against LLaDA2.1-16B Q-Mode, the ablation on lookahead steps, the analysis of proposal quality, and any qualitative or quantitative evidence of selective editing. Those parts tell you where the gains come from.

If time is limited, read the introduction, the theory summary figures, the method figure, the main results table, and the key ablations; that should take around 40–60 minutes. If you plan to build on this line of work, read the appendix as well, especially the complexity proofs, training details, and the implementation of proposal generation and conditioning.2d:T49f,PONDER frames sequential masked generation as an MDP.
- State: the current partially filled canvas x^(t) (visible patches as tokens, missing patches as MASK).
- Frozen generator: a backbone produces per-patch features from x^(t); a diffusion/continuous head fills selected patches.
- Policy actions: choose a set of patches to unmask and generate next; optionally choose previously generated patches to re-mask so they will be regenerated later (“rethinking”). This explicitly models revision rather than hoping later steps fix early mistakes.
- Training: keep the generator fixed; train only the policy with RL using a terminal reward computed on the final sample. Crucially, the method does not need token probabilities or exact log-likelihoods from the generator, which is what makes it applicable beyond discrete masked LMs.
- FIDgrad reward: approximate each sample’s marginal contribution to FID by linearizing the FID objective in Inception-feature mean/covariance statistics, yielding an image-level scalar reward usable by policy gradients.
At inference, a rethinking budget R can be adjusted to trade compute for quality while keeping both generator and policy fixed.2e:T89e,方法核心是 Sep-Latent。整体训练是一个从显式 CoT 逐步过渡到隐式推理的 curriculum。作者观察到分隔符 token，例如换行、逗号、句号，在注意力里天然容易成为结构汇聚点，于是把它们当作 semantic anchors。

第一部分是 Attention-Decay。做法是在显式 CoT 路径中，对非分隔符的 step tokens 施加逐步增强的 attention suppression。直观上，模型原本可以直接在每个推理词上保留和传播信息；加入 decay 后，这些普通 token 的可访问信息通路被压窄，模型被迫把关键语义压缩到相邻的 separator hidden states 上。这样，separator 不再只是标点，而变成承载步骤摘要的 latent carrier。这个设计和直接引入额外 latent token 不同，它复用了原始词表中的结构 token，因此不需要额外定义固定长度的隐变量槽位。

第二部分是 dual-path distillation。论文同时保留显式路径和隐式学生路径，并在 token-level 与 sequence-level 做多层蒸馏对齐。显式路径提供可监督的 CoT 轨迹，隐式路径学习用更少的 latent anchors 复现这些推理状态。作者强调 online-policy distillation，即蒸馏对象来自模型自身当前策略生成的 latent trajectory，而不是完全离线的教师缓存。这一设计据称能降低训练内存开销，也让学生更贴近推理时真实会走到的状态分布。

第三部分是 Dynamic Implicit Exit。模型学习一个退出信号，根据当前问题复杂度和内部推理状态决定何时停止 latent reasoning 并输出答案。相比固定 latent 步数，这让简单问题可以更早结束，复杂问题保留更深的内部计算。

从建模角度看，这篇工作的关键不是提出新的 backbone，而是把“结构 token + 注意力约束 + 双路径蒸馏 + 动态退出”组合成一个隐式推理训练框架。它与 Coconut/CODI 的主要区别在于：latent 容量不再由固定数量的专用 latent token 决定，而是由输入中自然出现的 separator 及其压缩后的表示来承载；同时用 attention-decay 主动塑造信息流，而不是只靠蒸馏目标被动学到压缩。2f:T77e,Sep-Latent is a curriculum that transitions from explicit CoT to implicit reasoning. The central observation is that separator tokens such as newlines, commas, and periods already act as structural aggregation points in attention. The method amplifies that tendency and turns those tokens into semantic anchors.

The first component is Attention-Decay. During training on the explicit reasoning path, the model progressively suppresses attention to non-separator step tokens. This narrows the information pathways through ordinary reasoning words and forces the model to route and compress useful intermediate information into the hidden states of separator tokens. In effect, separators become compact carriers of step-level reasoning summaries. This differs from methods that introduce a fixed number of dedicated latent tokens: Sep-Latent reuses natural vocabulary items and lets the compression structure emerge around them.

The second component is dual-path distillation. An explicit path with textual CoT is kept as a supervised reference, while an implicit student path learns to reproduce the reasoning trajectory using compressed latent anchors. Distillation is applied at both token and sequence levels. The paper further uses online-policy distillation, meaning the model distills from its own current latent trajectories rather than only from an offline teacher cache. The claimed benefit is lower memory cost and better alignment with the states encountered at inference time.

The third component is Dynamic Implicit Exit. The model predicts when to stop latent reasoning based on the current internal state and the difficulty of the query, instead of consuming a fixed latent budget for every example.

The novelty is therefore not a new backbone, but a training framework that combines structural-token anchoring, constrained information flow, explicit-to-implicit distillation, and adaptive stopping.30:T461,The evaluation covers math and commonsense reasoning benchmarks. The headline number in the provided text is 56.8% on GSM8K using only 5.4 tokens on average, with more than 2x better token efficiency than CODI and SIM-CODI. The paper’s claim is not that it reaches the highest absolute reasoning accuracy, but that it preserves competitive performance with much shorter reasoning traces.

Several supporting observations are reported. Attention-Decay is said to compress reasoning into separator anchors with negligible loss in perplexity and base accuracy. PCA visualizations suggest that the latent representations remain semantically diverse rather than collapsing into a narrow region, and that they stay grounded in the vocabulary space. Dynamic exit allows the amount of implicit computation to vary with task complexity.

From a foundation-model perspective, the experiments are more of a proof of concept than a scaling study. The paper demonstrates feasibility and efficiency gains, but it does not yet establish how robust the method is across larger models, different tokenizers, or broader training regimes.31:T5af,Causal Edit Serialization appends a structured edit stream after the source sequence. Each edit is decomposed into causal decisions: emit an operation token, localize a source position or span, and then emit payload tokens when needed. The supported operations are delete, insert, replace, copy, and move. Programs are delimited by edit-start and edit-end markers, and a boundary marker separates protected prefix from editable suffix. Edits are ordered left to right and refer to original source positions, so addresses do not shift after earlier edits are applied. The main mechanism is a pair of outputs: the vocabulary head selects a pointer role, such as replacement start or insertion location, and a lightweight localization head scores legal preceding source positions. When pointer tokens are fed back, a dual-index RoPE encodes both stream position and referenced source address. This lets the model condition on previously emitted pointers while preserving the usual causal attention mask. Training mixes ordinary language modeling with serialized repairs derived from random corruptions, model-generated edits, and mined copy examples. Compared with numeric-address edit scripts, CES avoids multi-token number generation and parsing. Compared with relative-distance vocabularies, it avoids committing to a fixed distance inventory. Compared with infilling or iterative editing models, it keeps the model in a single decoder-only causal format.32:T660,Two coupled components: a region-inhomogeneous forward process (training) and a detect–remask–refill sampler (inference).

1) Region-inhomogeneous forward dynamics
- Split positions into holes (to be generated) and user-provided context.
- Holes follow standard absorbing corruption over time t.
- Context follows a uniform-mixing corruption kernel at a small per-sequence rate η, which is equivalent to keeping context at a small, fixed “elapsed time” under uniform mixing while holes traverse absorbing dynamics.
- Training remains a masked-diffusion-style weighted cross-entropy denoising objective, but with modified forward marginals.
- Include an η=0 mixture component so the model still trains on perfectly clean conditioning, aiming to prevent degradation on clean inputs.

2) Detect–remask–refill with trust annealing
- Because context is sometimes corrupted during training, the model outputs a meaningful predictive distribution at every position, including the probability of the observed context token—used as a suspicion score.
- During early reverse steps, low-confidence context tokens are re-noised into the absorbing state (remasked) with an annealed intensity, then refilled by the standard reverse dynamics with bidirectional conditioning.
- After a lock time, context is frozen to avoid late-stage instability.
- The paper discusses confidence bookkeeping to compose this with low-confidence decoding.

Conceptually, absorbing diffusion is framed as one endpoint on a “trust axis” (infinite SNR for known regions); the method moves context to finite SNR so the model can doubt and revise it.33:T465,They evaluate corrupted-context infilling on web text with preregistered hypotheses and decision gates, and disentangle training-time vs inference-time contributions via nine experimental arms.
- Diagnostic: under absorbing dynamics, even uniformly random garbage context is treated as highly reliable; the pretrained model assigns on the order of ~50% probability mass to observed context tokens even when they are random, indicating a lack of a graded uncertainty mechanism.
- Results are strongest for conspicuous/uniform corruptions: finetuning under the new forward process yields better detection/repair/containment with no measurable regression under clean conditioning.
- For more plausible corruptions, detection is partial and infilling gains are small; the preregistered primary F1 gate fails.
- Ablations are not fully clean: the paper notes it does not completely isolate the effects of the η=0 mixture and trust annealing from other coupled changes.
- An offered (non-validated) interpretation: detectability and damage correlate with the divergence between the corruption kernel and the true data conditional.34:T9b1,方法上，论文先做了一个很干净的分解。作者把某个敏感分叉变量称为 fork，比如故事主角的性别、某个观点问题的立场。对于 fully masked canvas，只需一次前向，就可以直接读取模型在 fork 位置上的条件分布，把它定义为 model belief。作者证明并实证表明，这个 belief 与“从模型精确采样”是一致的，但成本远低于完整 sampling audit，文中给出的成本比是 1/11,520。这一步很关键，因为它把模型本身的偏好从 sampler 的影响里剥离出来了。

接着，论文分析 sampler 为什么会放大多数选项。核心区分是 commit rule 是否 peeking。所谓 peeking，是指 commit score 依赖于该位置刚刚采样出来的 token 身份，例如“采样到的 token 概率越高，越优先提交”。这种规则会让高概率 token 不仅更容易被采到，还更容易被保留下来，于是多数选项的 odds 被再次乘大。相对地，identity-blind rule 在决定提交哪些位置时，不看 proposal token 是什么，只根据位置本身的状态、熵或外部随机性来决定。论文给出形式化定义，并用一个 lemma 说明：如果 commit rule peeks，且提交概率随 token score 单调增加，那么更高概率的选项会得到额外的 odds amplification；identity-blind rule 则不会产生这类 token-channel 放大。

论文进一步指出还有第二条放大通道：ordering channel。即便 commit rule 本身不 peek，如果系统按 confidence order 先提交高置信位置，模型就会更早写入某些带有性别倾向或立场倾向的上下文，这些早期上下文又会反过来影响后续 fork 位置的条件分布。作者在职业故事场景里观察到，male-leaning context 往往在第一个 pronoun 之前被更早写入；而且每步 commit 的 token 越多，这种顺序偏置越强。

在干预方法上，作者提出 Fork-First Sampling（FFS）。思路很直接：在任何其他 token 写入之前，先从 model belief 或预设 target distribution 中抽取 fork 的值，再把这个已定 fork 的 canvas 交给任意 sampler 继续生成。faithful mode 用 belief 采样，目标是忠实于模型；fair mode 用目标分布采样，目标是控制 representation。FFS 只多一次前向，兼容 greedy decoding，也比“在 prompt 里显式指定性别”更自然，因为它不强行改写叙事内容，而是只控制关键分叉变量。35:T81e,实验覆盖 LLaDA-8B、LLaDA-1.5 和 Dream-7B，并在 occupational stories、GlobalOpinionQA、TANGO 以及一个已知真分布的 synthetic model 上验证。最醒目的例子来自引言：在固定 prompt 和模型下，LLaDA 默认 sampler 生成 female manager 的比例只有 21%，但模型本身对 female protagonist 的 belief 却是 66%。如果 sampler 完全忠实于模型，这两个数字不应出现如此大的偏差。作者还在 60 个职业上做回归，生成文本中的 female share 对 belief 的斜率达到 1.80，而精确采样应为 1。这说明 sampler 不只是有噪声，而是在系统性放大多数倾向。

论文把这种放大拆成两部分验证。对 token channel，作者比较 peeking 与 identity-blind commit rule，展示同一个位置若采到少数选项，其提交排名会显著下降。文中举的 LLaDA 单步例子里，采到少数代词 She 的位置，在 peeking 规则下 28 个候选里只排第 25，而在 identity-blind 规则下排第 3，因为后者不因 token 身份而惩罚它。对 ordering channel，作者分析在 confidence-based ordering 下，某些带性别倾向的上下文会在 fork 之前更早落盘，并且一次提交更多 token 时偏置更强。

FFS 的结果也比较扎实。用 fair mode 设定 50:50 目标后，在两类模型上都能把最终 fork 分布控制到距离目标 1.4 个百分点以内，同时 fluency 还有提升。faithful mode 则能让生成分布更贴近 model belief，避免默认 sampler 的额外放大。论文还强调，FFS 与 prompt-specified gender 不同，后者虽然也能控制表面属性，但常常损伤文本自然度或改变故事内容；FFS 因为只在生成初期固定 fork，后续内容仍由模型自由展开，所以文本质量更稳。

从实验结构看，最有说服力的是作者没有只做最终输出统计，而是先建立 belief 读取这一“近似 oracle”，再用它作为基准衡量 sampler 的偏差。这样可以把“模型本来就偏”与“sampler 把偏差放大了”分开讨论。36:T8e1,The paper first introduces a clean decomposition around a binary or categorical fork, such as a protagonist’s gender or an opinion label. On a fully masked canvas, one forward pass is enough to read the model’s conditional distribution at the fork position. This is treated as the model’s belief. The authors show empirically that this belief matches exact sampling from the model, while costing only 1/11,520 as much as a full sampling audit. This gives them a practical reference distribution that isolates the model from the sampler.

The main theoretical distinction is between peeking and identity-blind commit rules. A commit rule is peeking if the decision to commit a position depends on the identity of the token just sampled at that position, for example by favoring positions whose sampled token has higher probability. Such rules amplify majority options twice: they are more likely to be sampled and more likely to be kept. By contrast, identity-blind rules decide which positions to commit without looking at the sampled token identity. The paper formalizes this distinction and proves that under peeking rules, if commit probability increases with a score that increases with token probability, then the odds of the more probable option are further amplified. Identity-blind rules do not create this token-channel amplification.

The paper then identifies a second mechanism, the ordering channel. Even without peeking, confidence-based ordering can write gender-leaning or opinion-leaning context before the fork is resolved. That early context then shifts the conditional distribution at the fork position. In occupational stories, the authors show that male-leaning context tends to be written before the first pronoun, and the effect becomes stronger when more tokens are committed per step.

As a mitigation, the paper proposes Fork-First Sampling (FFS). Before any other token is written, the fork is sampled either from the model belief (faithful mode) or from a target distribution (fair mode), and the partially fixed canvas is then handed to any downstream sampler. FFS costs one extra forward pass, works even with greedy decoding, and gives exact control over the fork distribution without the awkwardness of prompt-level attribute forcing.37:T7c5,The experiments cover LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, and Dream-7B on occupational stories, GlobalOpinionQA, TANGO, and a synthetic model with known ground-truth belief. The headline example is striking: with the same prompt and model, LLaDA’s default sampler produces a female manager in only 21% of stories, while the model’s own belief assigns 66% probability to a female protagonist. Across 60 occupations, the slope of generated female share against model belief is 1.80, whereas exact sampling would yield a slope of 1. This shows systematic amplification rather than random deviation.

The paper validates both amplification channels. For the token channel, it compares peeking and identity-blind commit rules and shows that minority proposals are selectively delayed or discarded under peeking. In one real LLaDA step, a position that sampled the minority pronoun “She” ranked 25th out of 28 under the peeking rule, but 3rd under the identity-blind rule, because the latter does not penalize the proposal based on token identity. For the ordering channel, the paper shows that confidence-based ordering writes skewed context before the fork, and that committing more tokens per step strengthens this effect.

FFS performs well in both faithful and fair settings. In fair mode with a 50:50 target, the final fork distribution lands within 1.4 percentage points of the target on both model families, while also improving fluency. In faithful mode, generation tracks the model belief much more closely than the default sampler. The paper also argues that FFS is preferable to prompt-specified gender because prompt forcing can distort content or reduce naturalness, whereas FFS only fixes the fork and lets the rest of the story unfold normally.

A strong aspect of the experimental design is that the authors do not only compare final outputs. They first build a belief-reading reference and then measure how far each sampler moves away from it. That makes the attribution much cleaner.38:T5f7,Start with the introduction and the section on why samplers amplify majorities. That is enough to capture the paper’s main contribution in about an hour.39:T544,The model builds on Metis and keeps the idea of dynamic local memory plus trainable hyper memory. This is a sensible design choice: discrete or selective writing can introduce noisy credit assignment and brittle early training dynamics, while gated continuous updates allow every token to contribute with controlled strength. MemT-1.0 starts from a causal Transformer backbone and augments selected Transformer blocks with native memory blocks. Standard attention models the current context, while memory attention reads from the accumulated parametric memory. The excerpted content does not provide all per-benchmark numbers, so the tables and appendices should be checked for exact deltas.3b:T6c7,The paper has two parts: diagnosing the phenomenon and then intervening on training. For diagnosis, the authors build a synthetic task called Spaced Retrieval, designed to isolate retrieval ability from the messiness of natural language. The task uses controllable source-target gaps, with training and evaluation using t=5 and gaps of 64 and 8192 to represent short- and long-range retrieval. They then introduce a layer-wise contribution attribution method to quantify how much each layer contributes to retrieval over the course of training. The purpose is to track who learns retrieval first and who gets suppressed later. On top of that, they run freezing and unfreezing interventions. When recurrent layers are allowed to train normally, they acquire retrieval behavior earlier. When their retrieval learning is manually blocked, attention layers begin learning retrieval almost immediately. This is strong evidence that attention is not inherently incapable; it is being outcompeted. The paper further shows that the winner depends on data distribution: natural language contains many more short-range than long-range patterns, and recurrent layers learn those short-range patterns faster, which gives them an early optimization advantage that spills over into retrieval. To address this, the authors propose Better Layer Division (BLD), a training pipeline that adds a preliminary stage before standard pretraining. During this stage, selected components are frozen so that full-attention layers get an early window to learn retrieval first. Standard pretraining then resumes, but from a more favorable specialization trajectory. The key idea is not extra capacity, but changing the order in which modules are allowed to learn.3c:T54a,The experiments include both mechanism studies and end-to-end pretraining results. On the synthetic Spaced Retrieval task, the paper provides three kinds of evidence. First, layer-attribution trajectories show that recurrent/KDA layers take over retrieval earlier than attention. Second, freezing and later unfreezing gives a more causal result: once recurrent learning is stopped, attention’s retrieval contribution rises quickly. Third, changing the ratio of short- and long-distance patterns changes which mixer wins the competition, showing that the outcome is jointly determined by data distribution and learning speed. For realistic language modeling, the authors apply BLD to Kimi Delta Attention based hybrid LLMs at multiple scales and report gains over vanilla pretraining on training loss and several benchmarks, including commonsense reasoning, recall-intensive tasks, RULER, and LongPPL. The abstract does not expose all numbers, but the full paper argues that the gains are consistent across scales and not limited to one recurrent architecture. An important nuance is that the paper is not arguing recurrent layers should never do retrieval. The claim is that, under standard training, they learn it too early and too broadly, preventing attention from developing the specialization that would lead to a better overall division of labor.3d:T449,Read the introduction first and keep the target claim in mind: desirable specialization in hybrid models does not emerge automatically.
