All models are served locally through Ollama with temperature set to zero, specifically to avoid confounding effects from remote API guardrails.

The evaluation has two parts. First, they sample 200 prompts from each of five benign OR-Bench categories that are especially relevant to legal discourse: violence, sexual, harmful, illegal, and unethical. This isolates the “benign but safety-adjacent” regime. Second, they build a real-world corpus from Swiss Federal Supreme Court criminal judgments, extracting fact-section paragraphs and obtaining 1,652 aligned paragraphs across English, French, and German. This tests whether the effect survives outside synthetic benchmark prompts.

The main intervention is prompt prefixing. They compare no prefix, a lawyer prefix, a supreme-court prefix, and a jailbreak-style prefix. The legal prefixes are meant to reflect realistic workflow prompts rather than adversarial attacks. The jailbreak prefix serves as a control to test whether the model interprets legal authority framing as a role-play override. Refusal detection is done with an LLM judge based on Qwen2.5-14B. That choice is not the paper’s strongest component, but the experimental design is the real contribution: same request, same model, same decoding, only the framing changes; and the effect is tested across models, languages, and both benchmark and real legal text.150:T562,The headline result is that legal authority prefixes increase refusal rates by roughly 2.2x to 20x relative to the no-prefix condition, and this pattern appears across all four model families. The introduction also notes that ordinary legal-role framing can trigger more refusal than an explicit jailbreak-style prefix, which is a striking sign that the models are not merely reacting to obvious adversarial wording.

Two additional findings matter. First, the effect is multilingual but uneven: English, French, and German show noticeably different magnitudes. That suggests refusal boundaries are not language-invariant and may depend on training-data composition, alignment coverage, and prompt-template transfer. Second, the effect persists on real criminal-judgment text when the task is information extraction rather than open-ended answering. That makes the result harder to dismiss as a benchmark artifact.

From the available full-text content, the paper includes the right controls for a study of this kind: local inference to avoid platform-level moderation, deterministic decoding, prefix robustness checks, and a jailbreak comparison condition. What seems less developed is fine-grained error analysis. It would be useful to separate hard refusals, partial compliance with hedging, and safe-redirection behavior, and to report judge-human agreement more explicitly.151:T520,The paper introduces reasoning-aware multicalibration: keep externally important groups (e.g., topics that must be calibrated for policy reasons) and add internally important groups derived from observable CoT properties (uncertainty markers, revisions, self-checking, considering multiple answers, etc.). Then run a standard post-hoc multicalibration procedure (greedy iterative corrections such as iterative histogram binning) over the union of these groups.

A deliberate design choice is to use CoT signal as *group definitions* rather than as extra features for the base scorer:
- Calibration on topics is preserved by construction because the multicalibration constraints explicitly include them.
- The method is post-hoc: the generator and the initial scoring function are fixed, so it can wrap any existing confidence signal.
- Because calibrated scores are not used as rewards, the approach reduces incentives for CoT manipulation and is less sensitive to CoT unfaithfulness, as long as the observable properties remain statistically linked to errors.

The theory section formalizes when adding non-mandatory groups can reduce squared error, and identifies “internal importance” (groups that explain residual error beyond the mandatory groups) as a necessary condition—motivating CoT-based groups.152:T7a5,The model is a probabilistic context-free grammar defined on a fixed hierarchical tree. Sequences have fixed length over a discrete vocabulary, and the joint distribution is induced by hierarchical rules on the tree. Unlike experiments on neural LMs, the next-token conditional at each step is available exactly through belief propagation. This lets the authors cleanly separate the underlying language distribution from the decoding procedure: first compute the exact conditional, then apply a softmax temperature rescaling, and finally sample autoregressively.

The main observable is two-point mutual information. Because the hierarchical model is not translation invariant, the mutual information depends on absolute position as well as separation. The paper therefore focuses on the mutual information between the last token and the token located r positions earlier, which probes all hierarchical scales in a simple way. Across temperatures and grammar ensembles, the authors fit the decay of I(r) and test whether there is evidence for phenomena usually associated with criticality, such as a diverging correlation length, a transition from power-law behavior to a plateau, or a clear crossover to short-range exponential decay.

A notable part of the paper is the interpretation section. The authors give a tree-based statistical-mechanics view and an approximate mapping to an Ising model on a tree. This is used to explain why, in a fixed-tree hierarchical language, one should not expect finite-temperature correlation plateaus or the usual short-range exponential cutoff. Intuitively, the tree geometry itself induces multiscale dependence, while temperature mainly changes the strength of correlations and the fitted exponent rather than creating a sharp phase boundary. In that sense, the observed power-law behavior is better understood as a geometric consequence of hierarchical generation than as evidence of temperature-driven criticality.153:T67d,The experiments are numerical and deliberately clean. The focus is on correlation statistics, not task performance.

First, across the tested temperature range and multiple grammar ensembles, the two-point mutual information I(r) remains well described by a power-law envelope. Temperature changes the overall magnitude of correlations and also changes the fitted decay exponent, but there is no obvious special temperature at which the correlation structure changes qualitatively.

Second, this qualitative behavior is robust across different rule ensembles, although the detailed temperature response depends on the support structure and heterogeneity of the grammar rules. In other words, the exact exponent-versus-temperature curve varies with the grammar family, but the broader conclusion remains stable: power-law-like decay persists and no clear critical point appears.

Third, the Ising-on-tree analogy is used to interpret the numerical findings. In this finite-depth fixed-tree setting, the paper does not observe the standard signatures one would associate with true criticality, such as a diverging correlation length or a sharp phase transition. Therefore, changes in power-law exponents under temperature variation are not sufficient evidence for temperature-tuned critical behavior.

Start with the introduction to understand the target of the paper: it is not denying that temperature changes generation statistics, but questioning whether power-law behavior plus temperature sensitivity should be interpreted as criticality.

Then read the model and numerical protocol section. Three ingredients matter most: the fixed-depth hierarchical tree, exact next-token inference via belief propagation, and temperature applied only at decoding time. Once those are clear, the rest of the paper is straightforward.

If you care about language statistics, long-range dependence, or decoding temperature effects, the figures and appendix are worth reading carefully.155:T471,The method runs the model twice: once on the original prompt and once on a reference where the source tokens are replaced by EOS, while the response tokens and target span remain fixed. The scalar objective is the summed log-probability of the target response span. DeltaTrace decomposes the finite difference in that score. Instead of ordinary backpropagation, it builds operator-specific finite-change rules and propagates effective secant slopes backward through the computation graph. A token’s signed attribution is the inner product between its embedding displacement and the propagated secant slope. Local conservation ensures that token contributions sum to the observed score difference, and that aggregating tokens into sentences or passages preserves the interpretation. The derivations cover attention products, normalization, and Gated DeltaNet-style recurrent memory, so the same attribution idea applies to both attention and linear-attention models. The implementation uses FlashAttention-like tiling and Flash Linear Attention chunking to keep auxiliary storage linear in sequence length at fixed width and chunk size.156:T6a7,The main contribution is the controlled experimental setup. The task is SECDED ECC memory-wrapper generation, chosen because it is finite, parameterized, and formally verifiable. The authors define four output languages for the same design: fully expanded flat Verilog (L_raw), parameterized Verilog with generate loops (L_param), a parity-check matrix plus wrapper options (L_hmatrix), and an 8-field configuration expanded by a deterministic backend (L_cfg). For the widest design, the target length drops from about 44,237 tokens to 69 tokens, a roughly 640x compression.

They then compare seven training regimes: zero-shot, few-shot ICL, retrieval-augmented generation, LoRA SFT, full SFT, continued pretraining followed by SFT, and reinforcement learning from a formal verifier. This design is important because it separates representation choice from training recipe rather than conflating them.

A second technical strength is the leakage analysis. The encoder and decoder depend only on data width, so across 3,584 valid configurations there are only 8 distinct encoders and 8 distinct decoders. Random config-level splits therefore leak byte-identical substructures between train and test. The paper quantifies this and switches to width-disjoint splits, which is the right unit of generalization here.

Evaluation is also unusually rigorous. The oracle harness has five gates: lint, elaboration, self-checking simulation with exhaustive single-bit fault injection and random double-bit injection, formal equivalence against the reference, synthesis/PPA checks, and rejection of illegal configurations. That makes correctness decidable rather than estimated from a small handwritten testbench.157:T597,The empirical message is straightforward. First, output representation dominates training regime. As the target moves from long-form RTL toward compact configuration-level specifications, generation becomes much shorter, the error surface shrinks, and formal-equivalence rates rise sharply. On long representations, stronger training recipes help only modestly because the model still has to emit a large brittle artifact.

Second, naive data splits substantially overstate generalization. With width overlap, the train-test near-duplicate rate reaches 0.65–1.00 depending on the split, and the leakage worsens as corpus size grows. This is one of the most useful parts of the paper because it shows exactly how structural reuse can invalidate code-generation evaluation.

Third, once deployment cost is measured properly, compact-interface learning is far more efficient. A sub-50M model paired with the verified generator reaches 0.89 formal equivalence, while a 32B fine-tuned model reaches 1.00, but the smaller interface-learning setup uses about 1600x less inference energy per correct design. The point is not that small models beat large ones; it is that if a deterministic backend absorbs most of the implementation burden, model scale and training sophistication stop being the main bottlenecks.

The paper reports energy in joules per correct design, which is a much better deployment metric than raw pass rates alone.158:T659,The paper has three technical components. First, it performs a broad empirical audit of patch-token decoding across many pretrained ViTs. For classification models, intermediate patch tokens are passed through the final classification head and scored by the true-class logit. For contrastive VLM encoders such as CLIP and SigLIP, patch tokens are passed through the image projection head and compared against a text embedding like “a photo of a C,” producing patch-level similarity maps. These maps are then evaluated by comparing scores inside the object region versus the background, allowing the authors to categorize models into aligned, inverted, or unexplainable regimes. Second, the paper runs controlled synthetic experiments where architecture is held fixed or nearly fixed while task structure, loss, data distribution, and training conditions are varied. The central finding is not that one factor deterministically controls explainability, but that these factors change the optimization bias: they alter which among multiple functionally valid solutions training is more likely to find. Third, the paper provides a theoretical toy construction. It defines a simple classification task and a single-layer transformer for which the optimal classifier can be implemented in infinitely many ways. Some of those parameterizations are aligned under token decoding, while others are inverted. This elevates the empirical observation into a structural statement: even when the implemented function is the same, zero-shot decoding maps can differ radically because internal representations are not uniquely identified.159:T574,The experimental contribution is about breadth and consistency of the phenomenon rather than a single benchmark gain. The authors build Webdev-World, an executable environment that exposes code editing, application execution, browser inspection, and on-demand skills through a shared interface while preserving project state across interactions. Rewards are defined through a weighted checklist derived from task requirements. An independent verifier builds, runs, and inspects the final application. Deterministic checks and visual assessments are aggregated into a terminal reward, gated by successful execution and rendering. If the full paper includes ablations, the most important ones to inspect are the removal of progress signals, verifier gating, and cross-window training support.15c:T49e,The framework is called Harness-Policy Optimization (HPO). A coding agent is modeled as a pair of policy P and harness H, with trajectories scored by an executable verifier. Each round alternates two updates. In the H-step, the current policy is frozen and used to analyze its own failed trajectories, propose harness revisions, and select the best candidate on a search set. The harness can modify prompts, context organization, tool usage flow, feedback format, and stopping rules. In the P-step, the selected harness is frozen and the policy is updated with reinforcement learning under that harness. The updated policy then becomes the proposer for the next H-step. Crucially, the harness search set is also updated using hard tasks identified during the preceding policy-learning phase, so harness search stays aligned with the policy’s current weaknesses. The paper instantiates two versions: Self-HPO, where the evolving policy proposes its own harness candidates, and an external-model variant using Opus 4.8 as a fixed proposer. The main design insight is not merely “optimize both,” but to couple proposer identity and search-set construction to the evolving policy.15d:T410,The base policy is Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and the seed harness is mini-SWE-agent. Experiments are run on three coding benchmarks. The headline aggregate result is an average resolve-rate improvement from 57.8% to 64.8%. On SWE-Bench Verified, the base agent improves from 61.0% to 69.5% under Self-HPO, and to 71.6% when the same HPO loop uses Opus 4.8 as an external harness proposer. The gains transfer to out-of-distribution settings, including SWE-Bench Multilingual and SWE-Bench Pro. One of the most important ablations concerns the search set: dynamically updating it with hard tasks discovered during policy learning works better than reusing a fixed set. Another notable result is that Self-HPO improves both pass@1 and pass@k, which suggests it is not only making existing successful behaviors more reliable, but also expanding the set of successful trajectories the agent can reach. The provided text does not expose all RL details or per-round tables, but the paper states that average resolve rate improves at every optimization step.15e:T409,For a skim, start with the decomposition itself: policy defines the capability boundary, harness determines how that capability is elicited. A deeper read is only necessary if you want to port the idea beyond coding agents, in which case the definition of the harness search space becomes the key detail.15f:T6b4,The method starts with diagnosis. A behavioral checker replays successful trajectories, tracks repository state and required checks, and labels actions that go beyond what the task requires. The first such action in a successful run is treated as the onset of over-defense. By resampling from the same prefix, the paper shows that these points are silent forks: the next action can vary in proportionality while preserving success.

The paper then explains why a straightforward RL fix is weak. One can add checker-based penalties to the trajectory reward, similar in spirit to length-controlled RL. But that signal reaches a given fork only through trajectories that remain proportionate at all relevant forks. As trajectories get longer, such fully proportionate rollouts become rare. Under GRPO, which updates from within-group reward differences, many rollout groups become reward-identical, so the policy receives little or no learning signal.

The proposed solution is ForkDPO, a fork-level preference optimization scheme. Instead of inferring credit from outcome, it directly constructs preference pairs at the behaviorally meaningful fork. There are two pair types. One targets over-defense: the checker identifies the first disproportionate action in a successful trajectory, and the model is resampled from the same prefix to obtain a more proportionate alternative. The other targets under-checking: when immediate submission would skip a required check, the method also creates pairs on that side, so the model does not simply learn to check less. DPO is then applied to these fork-level pairs. The key difference from random-turn DPO is precise signal placement at the actual behavioral branching point.160:T618,The empirical story has three parts. First, the diagnosis: on a 4B model and four frontier models, silent forks are shown to be where over-defense begins. Under implicit budgets, when models are prompted from these fork prefixes, they choose the disproportionate branch in up to 91% of decisive actions such as testing, checking, or submitting. The paper also notes that both branches usually leave the repository unchanged and that over-defensive runs succeed as often as other runs, which directly supports the claim that outcome does not distinguish behavior quality here.

Second, the failure of reward-based fixes: when the checker is folded into the trajectory reward and training is done with GRPO, 71% to 74% of rollout groups under implicit-budget settings receive identical rewards, so relative updates largely vanish. After 12 rounds, the disproportion rate does not meaningfully improve. Random-turn DPO also helps little, indicating that the issue is not merely the absence of preference data, but the location of that data.

Third, ForkDPO improves behavior on 48 test tasks from unseen repositories. For the 4B model, the implicit-budget disproportion rate drops from 70.3% to 58.9%, an 11.4-point reduction. Median runtime falls from 143 seconds to 90 seconds, roughly a 37% decrease. Random-turn DPO only reaches 67.7%. The ablations also argue that both sides of the behavior boundary matter: penalizing over-defense alone can push the model toward insufficient checking, while adding pairs for required checks stabilizes the target behavior.161:T52b,Start with the introduction and the first motivating figure. A first pass should take about 35 to 50 minutes; if you work on agent RL or process supervision, the checker design and pair construction are worth a slower second read.162:T8ce,技术方案分成两层。第一层是 execution-verified training environment。作者在真实仓库的容器化副本中植入已知弱点类别，并要求只有当现成 exploit harness 能打通时，这个样本才被纳入训练。这样得到的不是“猜测这里可能有漏洞”，而是“这里存在一条可达 exploit path”的可验证样本。Red 的任务是在给定开发任务的前提下编辑 reference diff：对于 vulnerable scenario，要引入一个可利用且可达的 weakness，同时保证补丁能应用、能构建、能通过测试、还能完成原开发任务；对于 clean scenario，则做规模相近但不引入漏洞的编辑。Blue 则像代码审查模型一样，不只要判断 vulnerable/clean，还要定位 entry point、critical operation 和中间 trace，输出对开发者可操作的定位信息。

第二层是 PRPO，Peer-Relative Policy Optimization。每一侧不是单个 policy，而是 N 个 LoRA adapter 组成的同角色种群，挂在同一个 frozen base 上，LoRA 参数量约为基座的 0.1%，便于低成本维护多策略与权重重组。每一轮固定一个条件 ω=(scenario, frozen opponent committee, decoding budget)，让同角色策略在相同条件下比较。作者把 same-role peers 放进 advantage baseline，而不是放进 opponent pool、reward shaping 或 learned critic。直观上，这样做的目的是让某个 policy 的得分反映“在同样对手、同样任务、同样预算下，它比同伴好多少”，从而把对手强弱波动和样本难度波动从梯度信号里扣掉。文章把这种收益称为 matched-population advantage，并给出 advantage variance 的闭式分析。为避免种群退化，训练中还有 tournament 机制：淘汰最弱 adapter，并从较强策略重播种，维持策略多样性。

还有一个设计值得注意：这是非零和游戏。Red 不能靠生成无法构建或无法通过测试的垃圾补丁来“骗赢”，因为 reward 由执行验证决定，必须同时满足功能正确与 exploit 可达。这个约束很关键，它把攻击者从“让 Blue 犯错”改成“生成真实、可部署、难检测的危险改动”，使训练信号更接近实际代码代理场景。163:T8a4,The method has two layers. The first is an execution-verified training environment. The authors instrument known weakness classes into containerized copies of real repositories and only admit a site if an existing exploit harness can actually fire. This yields samples with executable ground truth: not merely that a vulnerability class is present, but that there exists a reachable exploit path. Red edits a reference diff that already completes a development task and passes tests. On vulnerable scenarios, Red must introduce one reachable weakness of the target class while preserving functionality. On clean scenarios, Red makes a similarly sized edit that introduces no weakness. Blue acts as an LLM code reviewer: it must classify the patch and localize the entry point, critical operation, and trace, which makes the output actionable rather than purely binary.

The second layer is PRPO, Peer-Relative Policy Optimization. Each side is a population of LoRA adapters over one frozen base model, with adapter size around 0.1% of the base parameters. A training round fixes a condition consisting of the scenario, a frozen committee of opposing policies, and a decoding budget. Same-role policies are then compared under identical conditions. The key idea is to place the population inside the policy-gradient baseline rather than in the opponent pool, reward shaping, or a learned critic. Intuitively, a policy is rewarded for outperforming peers that faced the same task, same opponents, and same budget, which removes some variance due to opponent strength and instance difficulty. The paper calls this the matched-population advantage and provides a closed-form analysis of the resulting advantage variance. To avoid strategic collapse, the population is maintained with a tournament mechanism that retires weak adapters and reseeds them from stronger ones.

An important design choice is that the game is non-zero-sum. Red cannot win by producing broken code that fails to build or fails tests. Rewards are execution-verified, so Red must generate patches that are functional, exploitable, and difficult for Blue to detect. That makes the training signal much closer to realistic code-agent deployment.164:T69a,The experimental program is organized around five questions: whether the attacker is reliable enough to train against, whether co-evolution beats static training, whether the detector transfers to unseen applications and languages, whether weight updates are necessary, and whether a population helps under a fixed verifier budget. The paper evaluates at least on code security and jailbreak safety, with the code-security side using VulnGym and comparing against supervised baselines, within-policy baselines, frontier-model baselines, and published agent baselines.

The main empirical story is clear from the full text. First, the execution-verified attacker is not just generating noisy adversarial examples; it can reliably produce patches that apply, build, pass tests, and reproduce real exploits, which makes it a viable online training opponent. Second, co-evolution outperforms static defender training, and the adapting opponent matters. If the attacker stops improving, Blue’s training reward can still rise, but held-out evaluation against an external attacker or historical opponents does not show the same gain. Third, the population design helps at a fixed verifier budget, which the paper analyzes in terms of estimator effect versus allocation effect. Fourth, inference-time search alone is insufficient; actual weight updates provide additional benefit. - Asynchronous architecture: on a single 8×B200 node, 2 GPUs train the policy while 6 GPUs run independent vLLM inference engines that keep generating rollouts while training proceeds. Weights are refreshed after every update, so a single multi-turn trajectory can span multiple policy versions.
- Off-policy control: a max_off_policy_steps threshold bounds policy staleness; rollouts exceeding it are dropped.
- Consistency constraints: align training and inference engines (tokenization, numerical/logprob paths) and maintain consistent cached state across policy updates to prevent importance ratios from being corrupted by implementation mismatch.

The server maintains a shared skill document d and a global experience document e. Each client has private train/validation splits and four LLM-based roles: an executor for task execution, a skill optimizer for local refinement, a sanitizer for privacy cleaning, and an auditor for private-value checking. Instead of uploading a rewritten full skill document, the client generates semantic commits: localized skill patches together with supporting experience summaries.

The pipeline has several stages. First, local skill evolution: the client executes tasks using the current global skill and global experience context, collects local successes and failures, and asks the optimizer to produce revisions. Second, two-stage privacy filtering: a sanitizer rewrites or removes sensitive content, and an auditor checks whether the commit still contains private values or environment-specific details. This is not formal differential privacy; it is semantic privacy filtering performed by LLM agents. Third, cross-round experience reuse: the server maintains a global experience document that accumulates reusable evidence over rounds and redistributes it to clients, reducing redundant rediscovery and making local optimization more informed. Fourth, experience-aware aggregation: the server uses a merge agent to combine commits with reference to the global experience document, rather than simply concatenating or voting over full documents. Fifth, version validation: a candidate updated skill is only published if it passes validation.

Relative to straightforward federated baselines, the key differences are the shift from document-level to commit-level updates, the inclusion of evidence alongside edits, and the explicit use of a shared experience memory. That makes the system closer to collaborative knowledge editing with validation than to standard federated averaging.16b:T63a,The paper reports experiments on three datasets and three LM families. The excerpt provided here does not include the full experimental tables, exact model sizes, or dataset sizes, so precise numbers beyond the reported “up to 22%” should be checked directly in the original paper before citation.16c:T46d,LEASH formulates weak-to-strong escalation as a budget-constrained sequential stopping problem, where the weak model’s estimated failure risk acts as a proxy for the benefit of escalation. It builds a representation bank from a small set of held-out tasks by recording hidden states on prompt and action tokens and labeling them with task-level and subgoal-level outcomes. At test time, the current prompt or execution trace is scored by a Mahalanobis-distance criterion: the hidden state is uncertain if it lies closer to past failures than to past successes. This score drives two mechanisms. First, an initial gate decides whether to escalate at the start, while a runtime gate monitors the weak agent during execution. Second, after handoff, the weak model becomes a shadow observer for the strong model, checking the trajectory every three steps. If uncertainty is high, the pending action is rolled back and re-decided once with higher reasoning effort. The main difference from prior escalation schemes is that no additional monitor training, external knowledge base, reference model, or per-step multi-sampling is required.16d:T80b,The framework is a sequential-auction MDP. A task is modeled as a finite-horizon MDP, but actions are not chosen by one global policy. Instead, a society of agents bids for the right to act on the current state. The winning agent transforms the state and then resells the resulting state into the next auction. When the task reaches a terminal solution, the final reward is propagated backward through the resale prices, implementing a bucket-brigade style temporal credit assignment.

The starting point is the theory of Chang et al., where Vickrey auctions align local bidding incentives with the globally optimal MDP policy under perfect competition. The paper argues that this assumption is economically unrealistic for LLM societies. With exact clones, the winner pays essentially its true valuation, so expected profit goes to zero and participation becomes irrational. At the other extreme, if an agent is the only eligible buyer at some step, it behaves as a monopsonist and bids the minimum needed to win. The clearing price collapses, upstream contributors are underpaid, and the multi-step chain becomes unsustainable.

The proposed shift is to study imperfect competition. Agents are similar enough to compete, but differentiated by inference cost, prompting, heuristics, and capability. Since LLMs are poor zero-shot estimators of their own success probabilities and token costs, the paper does not rely on direct self-evaluation. Instead, each agent learns a lightweight valuation policy with reinforcement learning to decide whether to bid and how much to shade its bid. The paper benchmarks four bidding strategies: Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO. It also compares multiple auction rules, including first-price, second-price, and a credit-conserving Vickrey variant.

Methodologically, the contribution is less about one new algorithm and more about building an experimental framework that combines sequential auctions, LLM agents, learned valuation policies, and market-density analysis under imperfect competition.16e:T4ed,The experiments have two roles. One is to validate the economic failure mode: in synthetic settings, the authors show monopsony failure, where lack of competition collapses bids and prevents value from flowing upstream. The other is to test whether realistic intermediate regimes work: they run market-density sweeps and compare decentralized markets against centralized orchestration baselines on task success and agent profit.

The domains mentioned in the paper include math reasoning and a newly constructed synthetic news market. The main empirical conclusion is that no competition fails, but perfect clones are not required either. A middle regime of imperfect competition is sufficient to sustain positive profits while also achieving higher task success than centralized orchestration baselines. That is the main result to retain.

First is a retrieval-based labeling pipeline. Starting from a corpus of user sessions, the system uses an off-the-shelf memory extractor (mem0 in the paper) to produce atomic candidate facts from each session. Under an infinite-budget construction, all extracted facts are added to a growing candidate memory pool. For each candidate fact, the pipeline scans future user turns. A turn is first judged on whether memory is needed; if memory is queried, retrieval is performed. A fact is labeled useful if it is retrieved in a later interaction and its content is actually incorporated into the model’s answer. An LLM judge is used to verify that the retrieved fact was genuinely used, reducing noise from superficial retrieval hits.

Second is Warm-Start UCB. The offline stage learns a shared utility pattern from historical users, providing a prior or initialization. The online stage adapts to a new user with an upper-confidence-bound algorithm under one-sided delayed feedback. Because feedback is observed only for admitted facts and only after an unknown delay, the problem is cast as an apple-tasting style decision process. UCB handles the exploration–exploitation trade-off by favoring facts with both high predicted value and high uncertainty. Compared with pure offline supervision, this explicitly models partial and delayed feedback. Compared with a cold-start contextual bandit, warm start uses population data to avoid learning each user from scratch.173:T4ba,From the provided full-text excerpt, the evaluation is built on PerMemBench-S and an additional longer-horizon synthetic benchmark, PerMemBench-L. Details on distillation data/trajectory construction and tool-use supervision are not present in the excerpt and should be verified in the full training section.175:T404,Retrieval Program Learning lets the policy write short executable programs instead of invoking one monolithic retrieval tool. These programs run in a sandbox and can use local state and control flow to combine search primitives such as dense retrieval, sparse retrieval, candidate filtering, deduplication, fusion, reranking, and evidence selection. The main training issue is sparse-reward exploration: useful programs may require several coordinated structural choices before answer correctness improves. The proposed solution is program mutation. Starting from suboptimal RL rollouts, a typed grammar generates nearby program variants while preserving the original queries. Mutations can change the retriever, increase retrieval breadth, merge result sets, or add reranking. Verified successful variants are converted into synthetic trajectories, briefly used for fine-tuning, and then RL resumes. This gives the policy structured experience with useful retrieval programs that pure on-policy exploration may rarely discover.176:T78f,LMMR has four main components. First, it builds a shared concept space across modalities. Instead of converting images into text summaries, it projects textual hidden states and visual patch features through modality-specific projectors into a shared sparse autoencoder dictionary. Sparse activations in that dictionary serve as common semantic addresses. This is meant to preserve more visual fidelity than captioning while providing a more structured alignment layer than raw embedding similarity.

Second, those shared concept addresses are used to build a query-conditioned memory graph. Visual evidence is linked to its dialogue turns, timestamps, and session context, so the system can reason not only about relevance but also about temporal validity. This is a key distinction from flat multimodal retrieval: the model must decide which state of an entity is currently valid, not merely which past observation looks related.

Third, the graph is encoded to aggregate cross-modal and temporal dependencies, while native visual tokens are still retained in the multimodal prefix. This dual path is important: concept abstraction organizes evidence, but raw visual tokens preserve details that abstraction may discard. The graph readout is then injected as a residual into a continuous latent rollout, allowing the model to integrate textual, visual, and temporal evidence in latent space before a grounding token returns the process to lexical generation.

Fourth, the overall design is neuro-symbolic in a restrained sense. The symbolic part is not a hand-written logic engine, but a sparse concept-address layer plus graph structure that makes evidence composition more explicit. The neural backbone still performs the final fusion and generation. Compared with flat cross-modal fusion, the main novelty is treating memory organization as a separate stage rather than simply concatenating retrieved items into the model context.177:T4a5,The evaluation uses Mem-Gallery and MemEye, covering nine long-term memory task categories and twelve settings with varying visual-detail requirements and memory complexity. First, LMMR improves over textified-memory approaches on tasks that require fine-grained visual grounding, because it avoids premature compression of visual evidence. Second, it improves over native-image retrieval baselines on tasks involving state changes and cross-session evidence integration, because it explicitly models temporal relations and current validity. Third, the query-conditioned memory state itself appears to matter: the gain is not only from better retrieval, but from organizing retrieved evidence before answer generation.

The paper is really about distributional assumptions in training signals. Many RL and post-training setups optimize behavior under idealized interaction conditions, so the learned policy becomes good at acting when information is complete, not at recognizing when information is missing. That is closely related to familiar pretraining concerns: train-test mismatch, idealized supervision, and the gap between surface data variation and the latent state the model actually needs to infer. The main contribution is not just showing that weak users hurt performance. The stronger result is that replacing strong-user training data with weak-user data does not automatically produce robustness. This points to an objective-design problem rather than a pure data-mixture problem. StaGPO is interesting because it uses an explicit intermediate state representation as a grouping device for step-level credit assignment, which may matter for RLHF-style training, tool-use RL, and other settings where outcome-only rewards are too coarse.179:T75a,There are two main technical pieces. First is the weak-user protocol. Instead of changing the simulator prompt, which would confound user knowledge, intent, and style, the paper applies post-hoc channel degradation. Each user reply is split into sentences, and each sentence is independently replaced by [inaudible] with probability p in {0, 0.2, 0.4}. The simulator itself still sees the unmasked history, so it behaves like a real user who assumes they already communicated the needed information. Only the agent receives the degraded text. This design is important because it preserves the underlying task and user state while giving the researchers access to both the original utterance and the observed one. That enables controlled cross-evaluation and counterfactual forks to trace which missing information caused failure.

Second is State-Grouped Policy Optimization (StaGPO). Standard GRPO assigns the same dialogue-level advantage to all turns in a rollout, which is too coarse when success depends on noticing a missing slot at the right moment. StaGPO asks the agent to write an explicit state before each action, describing what the task requires from the user, what information is still missing, and how each gap is being filled. A notable design choice is that this written state is not optimized as a direct auxiliary target. The appendix shows that rewarding repair actions is too sparse, and rewarding state accuracy can conflict with task success within a state group. Instead, the written state is used as a grouping key. Turns from different rollouts that reach the same need-gap-fill state are grouped together, and their discounted future returns are compared to derive a step-level relative signal without training a critic. The core idea is to align credit assignment across rollouts at the level of latent interaction state, not just final episode outcome.17a:T87c,The experiments cover two benchmarks, τ²-bench and ToolWOZ, with Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B policies, and evaluate all train-test combinations of strong and weak users. The first major result is negative but important. Weak users reduce success for every policy. On τ²-bench, a 4B policy trained with strong users loses 12.7 points when evaluated with a weak user at p=0.4 masking. More importantly, training on weak users does not fix the issue. Fixed-mask training, mixed strong/weak training, and curriculum variants all fail to outperform the strong-trained policy on weak-user evaluation beyond run-to-run noise, and some settings also reduce strong-user performance.

The paper also tests a natural intervention: prompt the agent to ask more questions after masked turns. This increases asking frequency by roughly 5x, but leaves task success essentially unchanged. Counterfactual fork analysis suggests that the issue is not insufficient questioning in aggregate; it is failure to identify the right missing field at the right time. The agent’s missing-information detection is poor: it marks about half of already-received details as missing, and even explicit hints about which fields are missing do not reliably improve behavior.

StaGPO shows clearer gains on ToolWOZ. When evaluated with the same user type used in training, StaGPO is at or above GRPO for every training mask and both model sizes. The paper highlights a +4.8 point gain for Qwen3.5-2B under weak-user training/evaluation. Transfer is also notable. A StaGPO policy trained with weak users is the best policy under strong-user evaluation and at an unseen mask rate, while a StaGPO policy trained with strong users serves weak users at least as well as a GRPO policy trained directly on weak users. On τ²-bench, gains are smaller but StaGPO still ranks highest under weak-user evaluation for both model sizes, with only a small margin for 4B. A skim takes about 35-50 minutes; a careful read with appendices is closer to 1.5-2 hours.17c:T92d,方法上分两层。第一层是攻击与评测设定的扩展。作者把 dormant poisoning 的目标从“生成有害文本回答”改成“在给定环境和任务上下文下采取有害动作”。这一步很关键，因为 agent 输出的安全性依赖环境状态，而不是单纯依赖文本表面。论文进一步展示了两个更强的风险：其一，经过 benign fine-tuning 激活后，有害倾向会泛化到训练时未显式植入的动作类型；其二，同一个模型里可以共存多个不同类别的 dormant harmful behaviors，并被同一次 benign fine-tuning 联合激活。

第二层是防御。作者先构造 Safety Buffer。每个 buffer 样本包含三部分：一个 harmful input、发布时模型对该 harmful input 的响应、以及一个保留上下文但去掉 harmful intent 的 benign version。这里的关键不是把发布模型输出当作绝对真值，而是把它当作“攻击者为了隐藏 poison 而必须维持的安全参考面”。例如 harmful input 可能要求从不可信链接安装软件，发布模型会拒绝或采取安全动作；对应 benign version 则改成打开官方软件下载页，要求模型在相同上下文下不要把拒绝模式泛化过去。

在此基础上，作者提出 LookAhead Defense。它不是像很多现有方法那样在每一步 fine-tuning 都持续加一个固定安全损失，而是先对 candidate downstream update 做 preview，再决定是否施加惩罚。具体来说，每个训练步先根据 benign downstream batch 计算候选更新；然后用 Safety Buffer 评估这次更新会如何改变发布模型原始响应在 harmful input 和 benign version 上的 likelihood。最后使用 one-sided objective：只有当更新预计会降低 harmful input 上安全响应的概率，或者提高 benign version 上拒绝式响应的概率时，才加 safety penalty。前者对应安全边界被削弱，后者对应 over-refusal 增强。这样做的动机很明确：只拦截“会破坏已知安全行为”的更新，而不对那些不影响安全边界的普通任务更新施加额外约束。与依赖 trusted clean reference model 的方法相比，它不需要外部干净模型；与依赖 externally provided safe responses 的方法相比，它不需要为 agent action 单独构造昂贵的安全答案。17d:T88c,The method has two layers. First, the paper extends the dormant-poisoning threat model from harmful text generation to harmful agent actions. This matters because action safety depends on task context and environment state, not just the surface form of a response. The authors show two stronger risks in this setting: benign fine-tuning can activate harmful behavior that generalizes beyond the exact poisoned action templates, and multiple distinct harmful behaviors can coexist in one model and be jointly activated by the same downstream fine-tuning process.

Second, the defense consists of Safety Buffer plus LookAhead Defense. Safety Buffer is built from the released model itself. Each example contains a harmful input, the released model’s response to that harmful input, and a benign version of the input that preserves context while removing harmful intent. The released model’s response is treated as a safety reference, not because it is guaranteed optimal, but because a successful dormant-poisoning attack must preserve apparently safe behavior at release in order to remain hidden. The benign counterpart is crucial because it prevents the defense from simply reinforcing refusal behavior everywhere.

LookAhead Defense then previews each candidate downstream update before committing to it. For a proposed fine-tuning step, the method evaluates how that update would change the likelihood of the released model’s response on both the harmful input and its benign version from the Safety Buffer. It applies a one-sided penalty only when the update is predicted to weaken safe behavior on harmful inputs or to increase refusal-like behavior on benign inputs. This is the key distinction from always-on safety regularization. The goal is to block only those updates that erode the preserved safety boundary, while leaving ordinary utility-improving updates mostly unconstrained. Compared with defenses that require a trusted clean reference model, this approach is self-referential and easier to deploy. Compared with defenses that rely on external safe responses, it is better suited to agent actions where safe behavior is context-dependent and expensive to annotate.17e:T61b,The evaluation spans standard language models, language agents, and multimodal agents. The models include Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct for language-model experiments; Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Granite-4.2-8B for language agents; and Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct for multimodal agents. Benign downstream fine-tuning uses GSM8K, Glaive, and OS-Genesis, respectively. This setup is useful because it tests the threat beyond a single QA benchmark and into action-taking and multimodal settings.

The main empirical findings are threefold. First, dormant poisoning does transfer to language and multimodal agents, and benign fine-tuning can activate harmful actions in these settings. Second, the activated behavior can extend to unseen actions, which makes the threat more serious than a narrow template-specific backdoor. Third, multiple harmful behaviors can coexist in one model and be jointly activated. On the defense side, Safety Buffer performs comparably to or better than buffers built from a trusted clean reference model or externally provided safe responses, suggesting that the released model’s own safe behavior is a viable anchor. LookAhead Defense further improves the safety-utility trade-off relative to methods that apply safety objectives at every step, because it penalizes only updates predicted to weaken safety or increase over-refusal. Start with the introduction to understand how dormant poisoning differs from standard trigger-based backdoors and why agent outputs make the threat more concrete. Then focus on the method sections for Safety Buffer and LookAhead Defense. They solve two separate problems: where the safety reference comes from, and when a fine-tuning update should actually be constrained.

In the experiments, prioritize three comparisons. First, the evidence that activation holds across language, agentic, and multimodal settings. Second, the replacement study where Safety Buffer is swapped with prior references such as clean-model buffers or external safe responses. Third, the comparison between selective one-sided penalties and always-on safety regularization, especially on over-refusal and downstream utility. A skim should take around 40 minutes; a careful read with appendices is closer to 1-1.5 hours.180:T674,WildAWM starts from user personas and daily activities rather than from isolated app templates. It constructs an executable personal-computer world containing websites, desktop applications, MCP services, and local files, with stateful dependencies among them. On top of that world, it synthesizes XAI tasks that require agents to combine GUI interaction, command-line operations, and MCP tool use.

The main methodological contribution is the quality-control layer. Instead of relying on static LLM scoring, the pipeline uses execution-based multi-agent quality gates. Heterogeneous agents, built from different models and harnesses, actually execute the synthesized tasks. Their trajectories provide evidence for three properties: solvability, difficulty, and judge consistency. This is important because synthetic tasks often fail in two ways: they are superficially plausible but impossible under the generated world state, or they come with weak verifiers that produce noisy rewards.

A second notable idea is verifier stress testing via sycophancy probes. The authors inject deliberately incorrect outcome feedback and check whether the judge follows the misleading signal. This is a practical way to test reward robustness and is closely related to reward hacking concerns in RLHF-style pipelines.

Relative to prior work such as AWM, WebArena-Infinity, Gym-Anything, TMax, CUA-Gym, and CUA-Universe, the differences are clear: PC-level multi-interface scope instead of a single interaction mode, connected workspace instead of isolated apps, execution evidence instead of reference-only filtering, and an end-to-end open-source synthesis stack.181:T4de,The pipeline produces 341 environment-task pairs. Each task requires at least three interface types, and many are long-horizon workflows exceeding 100 agent steps. The difficulty is nontrivial: even GPT-6-Astra solves only about 60% of them, suggesting these are not low-complexity scripted tasks.

For training, the paper runs online RL on two Qwen models, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-4B, using an OpenCode CLI harness augmented with GUI and MCP tools. The key empirical claim is that training exclusively in these synthetic worlds improves performance on all eight out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agent settings. The paper’s emphasis is less on squeezing benchmark maxima and more on demonstrating transfer from synthetic interactive worlds to external environments.

The most important experimental signal is the role of the quality gates and verifier checks. Without execution-based filtering, synthetic tasks are likely to be either unsolvable or weakly verified, both of which would poison RL. Readers should pay attention to ablations around multi-interface requirements, removal of quality gates, verifier robustness, and the gain difference between the 4B and 35B-A3B models under synthetic-only RL.182:T620,NCE has three core components. First, it organizes the running context into addressable blocks. Each block is named by dedicated address tokens, and some blocks such as system prompts or tool declarations can be locked. Second, it defines an executable editing grammar inside the model vocabulary. The grammar includes address tokens plus operator tokens such as drop, rewrite, and append, together with composition rules for forming valid edits. A task-agnostic runtime maps each well-formed edit to exactly one context-state transition. This is the key design choice: edit semantics are not explained in the prompt or delegated to external tool schemas, but anchored in the model vocabulary and a fixed executor. Third, it builds supervision with a two-teacher pipeline. An offline teacher reads the full trajectory and assigns each block a release point, meaning the earliest turn after which the block can be safely edited because its role in the task has ended. An online teacher only sees the current context plus those release annotations and decides when and how to edit. The crucial training detail is evolving-context distillation: after an edit is generated at the end of a turn, the runtime executes it before constructing the next turn’s input and labels. This avoids conditioning future supervision on text that the model has already deleted or rewritten. The paper also includes a strong control baseline where the same edits are exposed as external tool calls, isolating the effect of native expression from the mere presence of an editing mechanism.183:T474,The evaluation covers four long-horizon agent benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and SWE-bench Pro. The method is implemented on LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse 69B-A3B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. On LongCat with a 256K context window, NCE improves success rates by about 4.8 to 6.3 points over the base model across all four benchmarks, while reducing token usage by 31% to 44%. That combination matters: the gains are not coming from simply retaining more context. Against a tool-call editing baseline trained on the same edits, NCE is ahead by 5.2 to 8.0 points, which is the paper’s strongest evidence that native editing grammar has value beyond generic context editing. The gains transfer to Qwen3.6 as well, with an average success-rate increase of 4.5 points and a 15% reduction in average token usage. The most informative ablations are likely the release analysis, evolving-context supervision, and native-grammar versus tool-schema comparison. Even from the headline numbers alone, the paper makes a fairly clear case that native context editing improves both task completion and context efficiency.184:T6c6,SCA builds a full pipeline around symbolic verification. First, it formalizes tool-call histories as first-order logic facts using predicates for calls, parameters, and returns. To prevent the SMT solver from inventing unsupported facts, it adds closed-world assumptions: each timestep has a unique call, and past parameters and return values are fixed and complete. Second, it mines candidate constraints from API documentation. An initializer agent focuses on one target API at a time, retrieves related tool definitions, and proposes executable rules covering provenance constraints, temporal dependencies, domain restrictions, and observable-state preconditions. The model outputs both a natural-language description and a corresponding Z3 expression. Third, it refines those rules using execution traces. This matters because documentation alone tends to produce overly strict rules and miss environment-specific dependencies. A refiner agent removes bad rules and adds missing ones based on observed successful and failed interactions. Fourth, it performs runtime intervention. At each tool call, the current history facts and the mined rules are checked with an SMT solver. If the conjunction becomes UNSAT, the current call violates at least one constraint. The system uses an unsat core for approximate attribution and intervenes only when the current call participates in the contradiction. Interventions come in two forms: natural-language warnings that ask the agent to retry, and automatic repair via MaxSMT when a unique valid replacement can be inferred. The design choice is deliberate: the verifier does not replace the agent’s planner, but guards the tool boundary where structural errors are easiest to formalize.185:T55d,The work has two layers. First, it operationalizes IFs and builds an annotated benchmark. The authors collect 1,828 traces from 9 MAS-benchmark configurations: 1,048 from MAST and 780 manually curated traces from WebWalker / MrlX on WebWalkerQA and BrowseComp-Plus. They use Gemini 3.1 Pro as an LLM judge to inspect traces step by step and flag candidate IFs, then validate annotation quality with human audits and cross-model re-annotation. On a stratified sample, 87.7% of reviewed IF annotations were independently retained by both human annotators, and none were jointly rejected; among IFs identified by at least 3 of 4 judges, Gemini covered 90.2%. Second, they turn IFs into actionable signals. They derive taxonomies of IF error types and absorption mechanisms through open coding, then run matched counterfactual replay: repair an IF while holding the rest of the trajectory as comparable as possible, and test whether the final outcome changes. Finally, they use IFs in two downstream ways: IF-based scoring for best-of-N trace selection, and IF-GRPO, a variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization that incorporates IF cost into the learning objective. The key distinction from standard outcome rewards or PRMs is that IF-GRPO explicitly optimizes against locally harmful-but-absorbed errors, exposing the trade-off between task completion and process quality.186:T50b,There are four results worth retaining. First, IFs are common and not reducible to final failure. Across the full corpus, 54.3% of successful traces and 75.2% of failed traces contain at least one IF; conversely, 24.8% of failed traces contain none. This directly shows that outcome labels miss substantial process variation. Second, the annotation pipeline is reasonably stable, though not perfect. In the human audit, 64 of 73 reviewed IF annotations were retained by both annotators, and none were rejected by both. In cross-judge analysis over 90 traces, 174 IFs were identified by at least 3 of 4 judges, and Gemini recovered 157 of them. Third, counterfactual replay suggests IFs are not merely descriptive artifacts: repairing an IF improves failure rescue by up to 46.2 percentage points over no-op replay. That is the strongest evidence that IFs correspond to actionable process states. Fourth, IF-based scoring improves best-of-N trace selection over existing process reward models, and IF-GRPO improves accuracy in 6 of 7 configurations while reducing IF cost per task in 3. The paper also surfaces an important tension: cleaner process behavior does not always translate into higher task success, which is exactly the kind of objective-design issue that matters in RL for agents.187:T560,Agima (Agentic Imagination) trains one omni model to play three roles:
- Policy: propose actions given current observation and goal.
- World model: generate the next visual observation (an imagined image) conditioned on the action.
- Reasoner/evaluator: compare imagined futures in language space and decide which action/plan to execute.

Two-stage training:
1) Supervised fine-tuning with interleaved trajectories that explicitly teach the model to treat imagined observations as valid context for continued planning. The paper uses three planning formats: (i) linear rollout (single imagined trajectory), (ii) counterfactual branching (branch on alternative actions at a step and reject failing branches), and (iii) forward thinking (imagine and compare longer candidate plans before committing).
2) Agentic RL using GRPO with only a binary success reward. No extra demonstrations are provided; RL shapes how the model allocates imagination and comparison—when to explore another plan, how many alternatives to branch, and where branching matters—while keeping generated images as context during planning.

A key design choice is “single model, shared interface” instead of separate policy and world models, so imagined vs. real observations can be swapped seamlessly and RL can directly sculpt the reasoning/search strategy rather than only the action distribution.188:T432,Benchmarks include Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, trained on easier instances and evaluated on harder settings excluded from training.

Reported highlights:
- With SFT alone, Agima generalizes from two-box to four-box Sokoban. Under sparse real feedback (real observation every 5 actions), it reaches 40% success vs. 2% for an action-only planner fine-tuned from the same backbone.
- “Forward thinking” improves long-horizon planning in Pacman even when trained on the same instances as linear rollouts, suggesting gains come from comparison/selection behavior rather than more data.
- GRPO further improves success and yields emergent planning organization not seen in SFT: e.g., in forward thinking it often imagines one plan first and only explores a second if the first is predicted to fail; in counterfactual branching it increases branching and concentrates it on critical irreversible decisions.

(Additional details like model size, compute, and full tables should be taken from the main results section; they are not fully present in the provided excerpt.)189:T8ba,论文的技术路线是把“数据选择”当成完整 pipeline 来评估，而不是只比一个打分函数：

1）对照组设计：repacking vs natural long docs
- repacking：把短文本拼成 128K 序列，长度满足但跨段依赖弱。
- random-long：从自然长文档池随机抽样，保留真实长文档结构（跨章节引用、延迟指代、分布式证据）。
- 关键发现是：random-long 在更长评测长度上更占优，说明“真实长依赖结构”比“仅仅更长”更重要。

2）在固定候选池内比较多类 selector
- generic-quality：PPL、gzip compressibility 等。
- LLM-judge：用大模型打分判断文档是否“适合长上下文训练”。
- likelihood/dependency-aware：包括 LongFilter、Prospector、以及 LongPPL key-token density。
- 论文强调所有自然长文档 selector 都在同一候选池上操作，避免“语料不同导致结论不同”。

3）LongPPL-density 与 truncLongPPL
- LongPPL 的核心是定义 key token：该 token 在长上下文条件下的 log-likelihood 相对短上下文显著提升（超过阈值 α，同时满足 β 等条件）。文档分数是 key token 的密度（比例）。直觉是：密度高的文档包含更多需要远距离信息才能预测的监督信号。
- full-span 计算昂贵（要在接近目标长度 L 的 span 上算长/短上下文对比）。论文提出 truncLongPPL：只在文档前缀的某个比例 r 上计算密度，用它近似全文排序。
- 这不是简单的“截断省算力”，而是验证了：对 128K 目标长度，算 reference span 的前半段就能保留大部分选择收益，并带来端到端 2.28× 的打分加速（文中写作 2.28× 2.28×）。

4）训练配方与控制变量
- Qwen2.5-3B 直接扩到 128K：通过把 RoPE base 提到 θ=2×10^8；bf16 + AdamW；常数 LR=1e-6；每步约 8M tokens；clip 1.0。
- 评测上用 HELMET 来决定选择配置，RULER 作为 held-out 长上下文评测；另有 7 个短上下文任务监控能力保持。
- 进一步做 256K 扩展、以及 short/long 混训（例如 66/34）来缓解 continued training 带来的短上下文退化，并在更大模型（Qwen3-8B、OLMo 3-7B）上验证趋势。18a:T8c1,The paper evaluates end-to-end selection pipelines rather than a single scoring heuristic.

1) Baseline pipeline comparison: repacking vs natural long docs
- Repacking constructs 128K sequences by concatenating shorter texts, satisfying length but typically lacking cross-section dependencies.
- Random-long samples genuine long documents, preserving delayed references and distributed evidence.
- The study finds random-long performs better at longer evaluation lengths, suggesting that real long-range structure matters more than mere sequence length.

2) Controlled selector comparison within a fixed candidate pool
Selectors fall into three families:
- Generic quality: perplexity, gzip compressibility.
- LLM-judge: a model-based “is this good long-context training data?” scorer.
- Dependency/likelihood-aware: LongFilter, Prospector, and LongPPL-based key-token density.
All natural-long selectors operate on the same candidate pool to avoid confounding from corpus differences.

3) LongPPL key-token density and truncLongPPL
- LongPPL defines “key tokens” whose log-likelihood improves substantially when conditioning on long context vs short context (thresholded by parameters like α and β). Document score is the density (fraction) of such tokens, aligning selection with documents that actually require long-range context.
- Full-span LongPPL scoring is expensive at scale. truncLongPPL computes key-token density on a truncated prefix (fraction r of the reference span) and uses it as a proxy for full-span ranking.
- Empirically, scoring only the first half of the reference span at 128K yields downstream performance close to full-span scoring, with an end-to-end scoring speedup of about 2.28×.

4) Training/eval controls
- Qwen2.5-3B is extended to 128K by increasing RoPE base to θ=2×10^8; bf16 + AdamW; constant LR 1e-6; ~8M tokens per optimizer step.
- HELMET is used to determine selection configurations; RULER is held out for evaluation; seven short-context tasks track capability retention.
- Additional validations include 256K extension, short/long mixing (e.g., 66/34) to mitigate short-context regression, and tests on larger backbones (Qwen3-8B, OLMo 3-7B), plus post-SFT checks (LongBench v2, MRCR).18b:T61d,Main controlled setting:
- Backbone/target: Qwen2.5-3B at 128K.
- Budget: 6B continued-training tokens per configuration.
- Candidate pool: sampled from 25% of an internal pretraining corpus; includes books, scanned docs, manuals, academic papers, web; multilingual (English/Chinese/mixed); excludes repo-level code. About 3M documents with length ≥128K tokens.

Key findings reported in the provided text:
- Random-long (natural long docs) outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths.
- Within the same natural-long pool, selecting by high LongPPL key-token density yields further gains; generic-quality selectors (PPL/gzip) and an LLM-judge selector do not match this improvement in the controlled setup.
- truncLongPPL: scoring only the first half of the reference span achieves performance close to full-span scoring at 128K, with ~2.28× end-to-end scoring speedup.
- Capability breakdown: gains are most consistent on retrieval-oriented long-context abilities; other capabilities show less uniform improvements.

Further validations (as described):
- 256K target context under the same training-token budget.

Engineering caveats highlighted by the study:
- Continued training for long context can hurt short-context performance; the mixed short/long recipe (e.g., 66/34) and the short-data source baseline (dolma3-short) are important for interpreting net gains.
- LongPPL-style scoring is compute-heavy; truncLongPPL is mainly about making dependency-aware selection scalable.18d:T689,The pipeline begins with outlet identification. Instead of crawling the web independently, the paper extracts pages directly from existing LLM pretraining corpora, namely English FineWeb and FineWeb-2. This design choice is important. First, in English web crawls, the share of state media pages coming from editorially controlled outlets rises sharply over time, from 39% in 2013 to 93% in 2025. This suggests that the English-language state media slice entering open-web corpora has become increasingly dominated by more tightly controlled sources.

Second, in several low-resource languages, state media accounts for a nontrivial share of all web data. The paper reports values up to 17.8% for Uyghur. For multilingual pretraining, this is important because when the total amount of web text is small, source concentration can have a much stronger effect on the learned distribution.

Third, the Russia-Ukraine case study shows that the issue is not merely ideological disagreement. Russian English-language state media covers international affairs broadly, while Ukrainian state media is more focused on Ukrainian affairs. On topics such as Crimea, the extracted factual claims and narrative framing diverge in systematic ways. This means that even when both sources look like ordinary news text, they provide very different world-model signals during training.

Fourth, in the RAG experiments, retrieval over foreign-targeted state media amplifies cross-lingual divergence in model responses on territorial disputes.
